meta.blurb: In legend, sacred geese wake the defenders of a hill at night, just as the Gauls begin to climb. It is one of ten moments, from a wolf and twins to the last western emperor, that show how Rome rose and fell.
meta.bible:
A single narrator tells the story of Rome through ten moments, twenty beats each, in two chapters of ten: 1 the founding legend (about 753 BCE), 2 the end of the kings (509 BCE), 3 the Gauls sack Rome (about 390 BCE), 4 Hannibal and Cannae (216 BCE), 5 Spartacus (73 to 71 BCE), 6 Caesar and the Rubicon (49 BCE) and the Ides of March (44 BCE), 7 Augustus, the first emperor (27 BCE), 8 Vesuvius and Pompeii (79 CE), 9 citizenship for all free people (212 CE), 10 the last western emperor (476 CE). Places: Rome, Tiber, Palatine Hill, Capitoline Hill, Italy, Gaul, Alps, Allia, Carthage, Cannae, Zama, Capua, Vesuvius, Pompeii, Herculaneum, Naples, Bay of Naples, Misenum, Stabiae, Rubicon, Actium, Egypt, Spain, Syria, Britain, Danube, Constantinople, Bosporus, Ravenna, Mediterranean, Thrace, Balkans, Persian Gulf. beats.scene: Seven low green hills beside a river bend, with a few huts
beats.summary: Rome grew on low hills beside the Tiber, in the middle of Italy.

beats.scene: A shallow river crossing where traders lead donkeys loaded with sacks of salt
beats.summary: A river crossing and the salt trade gave the place its chance to grow.

beats.scene: Round thatched huts on a hilltop, with smoke, goats and a child
beats.summary: The early Romans were farmers and shepherds living in small villages of huts.

beats.scene: A man carries his old father through a burning city towards ships
beats.summary: The Romans told a story that their ancestors came from the lost city of Troy.

beats.scene: A hero and his followers step ashore on an Italian beach at dawn
beats.summary: Aeneas reached Italy, and his descendants founded the town of Alba Longa.

beats.scene: A greedy younger brother seizes a crown from an older king
beats.summary: In Alba Longa, Amulius took the throne from his brother Numitor.

beats.scene: A priestess in white tends a sacred fire inside a stone temple
beats.summary: Amulius made his niece Rhea Silvia a priestess, but she bore twin sons.

beats.scene: A grim king points to the door as a servant lifts two babies
beats.summary: Amulius ordered the babies left to die by the river.

beats.scene: A basket rests in mud under a fig tree beside a flooded river
beats.summary: The flood went down and left the basket safe under a fig tree.

beats.scene: A historian writes at a desk among scrolls by lamplight
beats.summary: The tale was written down about seven hundred years later, so it is a legend.

beats.scene: A she-wolf feeds two babies in a shady cave while a woodpecker watches
beats.summary: A she-wolf fed the twins, and a woodpecker is said to have helped her.

beats.scene: A bearded shepherd lifts two babies out of a cave
beats.summary: The shepherd Faustulus found the twins and took them home to his wife.

beats.scene: Two strong young men herd sheep and wrestle on a grassy hillside
beats.summary: The twins grew up as bold shepherds, leaders of the young men of the hills.

beats.scene: An old man studies the face of a young prisoner in a hall
beats.summary: Remus was captured, the truth came out, Amulius died and Numitor won back his throne.

beats.scene: Two brothers stand on a hilltop and look down at a river valley
beats.summary: The twins left Alba Longa to found a city where they had been raised.

beats.scene: Two men sit on separate hills and watch vultures circling the sky
beats.summary: The brothers asked the gods for a sign: Remus saw six vultures, Romulus twelve.

beats.scene: A man drives two oxen as they plough a deep furrow round a hill
beats.summary: Romulus ploughed a furrow to mark the line of the city's wall.

beats.scene: A young man leaps over a low half-built wall while his brother glares
beats.summary: Remus mocked the low wall and jumped it, and in the best-known story Romulus killed him.

beats.scene: A crowned man welcomes a crowd of poor travellers through a rough gateway
beats.summary: Romulus became king and made his small city a refuge for runaways and newcomers.

beats.scene: Archaeologists brush the floor of an ancient hut on a hill
beats.summary: Archaeology fits the legend roughly, but nobody can prove that Romulus lived.

beats.scene: Seven crowned figures carved in a row along a stone wall
beats.summary: By tradition seven kings ruled Rome in turn, though historians doubt many details.

beats.scene: A gentle king in a white robe lights a flame in a small temple
beats.summary: Numa Pompilius, the second king, was a man of peace who shaped Rome's religion and calendar.

beats.scene: A warrior king leads soldiers past the burning walls of a hill town
beats.summary: Tullus Hostilius, the third king, destroyed Alba Longa and brought its people to Rome.

beats.scene: A wooden bridge crosses a broad river as barges carry salt towards the sea
beats.summary: Ancus Marcius, the fourth king, built a bridge over the Tiber and a port at its mouth.

beats.scene: A king in a patterned Etruscan robe sits on a carved chair
beats.summary: Tarquinius Priscus, an Etruscan, became the fifth king and brought new customs to Rome.

beats.scene: Workers dig a vast stone drain beneath a marshy valley
beats.summary: The kings drained the marshy valley with a great stone drain, and the Forum was born.

beats.scene: A king watches clerks count citizens, grouped by wealth, in an open field
beats.summary: Servius Tullius, the sixth king, counted the citizens by wealth and organised the army.

beats.scene: A stern king in purple robes stands over bowing nobles in a hall
beats.summary: Tarquin the Proud seized the throne from Servius and ruled by fear.

beats.scene: Labourers raise huge stone columns for a temple on a hilltop
beats.summary: Tarquin built a giant temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill with forced labour.

beats.scene: Angry citizens whisper in a dark street as royal guards pass
beats.summary: Nobles and ordinary people alike hated the king and waited for their chance.

beats.scene: A young noblewoman weeps before her father and husband in a candlelit hall
beats.summary: In the legend, the king's son wronged the noblewoman Lucretia, and she told her family.

beats.scene: A man in a plain cloak throws off his pretence and raises a knife
beats.summary: Lucius Junius Brutus swore with the others to drive the Tarquins out of Rome.

beats.scene: Roman citizens stand at a locked city gate while a royal chariot waits outside
beats.summary: The people shut the gates against Tarquin, and he was exiled, traditionally in 509 BCE.

beats.scene: Two men in white togas sit side by side with bundles of rods
beats.summary: Rome chose two consuls each year, and Brutus and Collatinus were the first.

beats.scene: One magistrate raises a hand to stop another from signing a scroll
beats.summary: Each consul could veto the other, and the Romans came to hate the very word king.

beats.scene: A lone soldier holds a narrow wooden bridge while others chop it down
beats.summary: The legend tells how Horatius held a bridge against the Etruscan king Porsena.

beats.scene: Senators in togas and a crowd of citizens gather below a banner
beats.summary: Rome became a republic, a public thing, run by its Senate and its people.

beats.scene: Rich men in white togas look down on poor labourers carrying sacks
beats.summary: In practice rich patrician families held most power, and the poor plebeians had debts.

beats.scene: A crowd of workers marches out of a city gate carrying bundles
beats.summary: In 494 BCE the plebeians walked out of the city and won their own officials, the tribunes.

beats.scene: Bronze tablets covered in small letters stand in the Forum while people read
beats.summary: About 450 BCE the laws were written on tablets in the Forum, so that everyone could read them.

beats.scene: Roman farmers and soldiers beside a growing town of stone and timber
beats.summary: By 400 BCE Rome had grown strong by beating its neighbours one town at a time.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers surround a walled hilltop city under a grey sky
beats.summary: About 396 BCE Rome took the Etruscan city of Veii after a long siege and won its rich land.

beats.scene: Tall warriors with long moustaches and painted shields stand beside wagons in a forest
beats.summary: The Gauls were Celtic peoples, farmers and warriors who lived beyond the Alps.

beats.scene: A long line of wagons and warriors descends a snowy pass into green plains
beats.summary: Gaulish tribes crossed the Alps in search of land and settled in northern Italy.

beats.scene: Three Roman envoys in togas stand among Gaulish warriors outside a walled town
beats.summary: The Gauls besieged the Etruscan town of Clusium, and in the story Roman envoys joined the fight.

beats.scene: A huge army marches along a dusty road beneath a clear sky
beats.summary: Brennus led the Gauls straight towards Rome, so fast that Rome had little time to prepare.

beats.scene: Two armies meet beside a small river below low hills
beats.summary: At the river Allia, eleven miles from Rome, the Gauls attacked and the Roman line broke.

beats.scene: Panicked soldiers throw down their shields and swim across a river
beats.summary: Many Romans fled to Veii, and some ran into Rome and did not even close the gates.

beats.scene: Families carry bundles and children through a city gate at dusk
beats.summary: Most Romans left the city, while the men who could fight went up to the Capitoline Hill.

beats.scene: Old senators in ivory chairs wait silently in a square as warriors approach
beats.summary: In the legend, old men who could not fight sat in their robes and waited for the Gauls.

beats.scene: Gaulish warriors walk through an empty street past open doors
beats.summary: The Gauls entered the empty city, took what they wanted and killed those who had stayed.

beats.scene: Flames rise above wooden roofs as warriors carry bundles through smoky streets
beats.summary: The Gauls burned much of the city, though archaeologists find the evidence thin.

beats.scene: Defenders on a steep rocky hilltop look down at the campfires of an army
beats.summary: The defenders held the Capitoline Hill, a steep rock with one hard path, for months.

beats.scene: Thin soldiers share the last bread on a rocky hilltop at night
beats.summary: Hunger and illness weakened both sides, and Rome's exiled general Camillus gathered an army.

beats.scene: Dark figures climb a steep cliff in silence under the moon
beats.summary: One night the Gauls found a path up the cliff and began to climb it.

beats.scene: Geese honk loudly in a temple garden while a soldier wakes
beats.summary: Sacred geese woke Marcus Manlius, who hurled the first climber down the slope.

beats.scene: Guards kneel in disgrace while a citizen receives gifts of grain
beats.summary: The failed guards were punished and Manlius was rewarded, and Romans remembered the geese for centuries.

beats.scene: A chieftain throws his sword onto a scale beside heaps of gold
beats.summary: The Gauls agreed to leave for a ransom of a thousand pounds of gold.

beats.scene: A Roman general in a plumed helmet leads fresh soldiers up a hill road
beats.summary: Roman stories say Camillus drove the Gauls out, but a Greek historian says otherwise.

beats.scene: Masons fit huge stone blocks into a long wall circling the hills
beats.summary: Rome was rebuilt in haste, a stone wall was raised, and no foreign enemy took the city for centuries.

beats.scene: A busy harbour of a rich city with tall ships, merchants and crates
beats.summary: Carthage, in North Africa, was a rich trading city with a mighty navy.

beats.scene: A wall map of Italy shows roads and towns joined into one network
beats.summary: By about 270 BCE Rome ruled most of Italy through allies and roads.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers land from boats on a sunny Sicilian beach
beats.summary: In 264 BCE Rome and Carthage began the First Punic War over Sicily.

beats.scene: Carpenters on a beach build rows of warships from fresh timber
beats.summary: Rome, which had no navy, built one in a hurry.

beats.scene: A warship rams its enemy while soldiers cross a spiked bridge to board
beats.summary: Roman crews used a boarding bridge to turn sea battles into land fights.

beats.scene: A fleet sails through rough water near rocky islands under tall banners
beats.summary: In 241 BCE Rome won the war, and Carthage left Sicily and paid a huge sum.

beats.scene: A stern general leads soldiers and ships to a silver-mining coast in Spain
beats.summary: Carthage built a new base in Spain under the general Hamilcar Barca.

beats.scene: A boy stands before an altar while his father watches
beats.summary: The story says the boy Hannibal swore never to be a friend of Rome.

beats.scene: A young general in armour looks over a walled Spanish city and the sea
beats.summary: At twenty-six Hannibal took command and besieged Saguntum, a city friendly to Rome.

beats.scene: Roman envoys in togas hold up a fold of cloth before a council
beats.summary: Rome declared war in 218 BCE, and Hannibal planned to strike at Italy by land.

beats.scene: A long column of soldiers and elephants leaves a Spanish port city
beats.summary: In 218 BCE Hannibal marched from Spain with a large army and thirty-seven elephants.

beats.scene: Elephants stand on rafts covered with earth to cross a wide river
beats.summary: He crossed the Rhône, ferrying the elephants on rafts.

beats.scene: Soldiers and elephants struggle up a narrow icy mountain pass
beats.summary: The crossing of the Alps took about two weeks in early winter, and many died.

beats.scene: A thin tired army looks down on the green plains of northern Italy
beats.summary: Hannibal reached Italy with perhaps twenty-six thousand men and won the first battles.

beats.scene: A Roman army marches in thick mist beside a lake while warriors wait above
beats.summary: At Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE Hannibal ambushed a Roman army in the mist.

beats.scene: A cautious general in a red cloak watches an enemy camp from a hill
beats.summary: Fabius, nicknamed the Delayer, avoided battle and wore Hannibal down.

beats.scene: Two lines of soldiers face each other on a flat plain, the centre curved
beats.summary: At Cannae in 216 BCE Hannibal drew the Romans in and surrounded them.

beats.scene: Roman senators in dark robes stand silent in the Forum after bad news
beats.summary: Rome lost tens of thousands of men but refused to make peace.

beats.scene: A Roman general stands on a hill above an African battlefield
beats.summary: Scipio carried the war to Africa and beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE.

beats.scene: A great harbour city burns while Roman soldiers watch from its walls
beats.summary: Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE and ruled the western Mediterranean.

beats.scene: Slaves carry water jars and sacks through a busy Roman street
beats.summary: By the first century BCE slavery was part of daily life, in houses, farms and mines.

beats.scene: Chained prisoners walk behind soldiers on a dusty road towards a market
beats.summary: Most slaves were prisoners of war, kidnapped people or the children of slaves.

beats.scene: Slaves bend over vines on a large farm, others dig in a mine
beats.summary: Slaves worked on huge farms and in mines, and some were cooks, teachers or doctors.

beats.scene: A master points sternly at a kneeling slave beside a locked door
beats.summary: A slave was a master's property with almost no rights, though some were freed in time.

beats.scene: A watchman peers anxiously from a farmhouse over dark fields at night
beats.summary: Some Romans feared slave revolts, and there had already been two on the island of Sicily.

beats.scene: Mourners at a funeral watch two armed men fight on a sandy floor
beats.summary: Gladiator fights began at funerals, and the first in Rome was held in 264 BCE.

beats.scene: Gladiators train with wooden swords in a walled sandy yard
beats.summary: Gladiators trained in special schools, and a famous one stood at Capua.

beats.scene: A strong Thracian fighter stands beside his wife in a stone cell
beats.summary: Spartacus, from Thrace, had once served Rome's army before he was enslaved and sold.

beats.scene: Gladiators whisper in a kitchen at night beside a rack of knives
beats.summary: About two hundred men planned an escape, but about seventy broke out with kitchen tools.

beats.scene: Escaped gladiators seize a wagon of weapons on a country road
beats.summary: They took weapons from a wagon, chose three leaders and camped on Mount Vesuvius.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers block the only path up a steep, rocky mountain
beats.summary: A Roman force blocked the only path up the mountain and waited for the rebels to starve.

beats.scene: Men climb down a cliff on ropes made of wild vines at dusk
beats.summary: The rebels made ropes of wild vines, climbed down the cliff and took the Roman camp by surprise.

beats.scene: Herdsmen and farm workers join a growing camp of rebels with stolen horses
beats.summary: News spread, and thousands of herdsmen and farm workers joined the rebels.

beats.scene: Roman officers retreat from a battlefield while rebels wave captured standards
beats.summary: The rebels beat several Roman forces, and for the first time the Senate felt real fear.

beats.scene: Two leaders argue over a map beside a fire while their followers watch
beats.summary: The rebels quarrelled about their aims, and Crixus left with his own followers and was killed.

beats.scene: A huge column of rebels, wagons and families crosses green hills heading north
beats.summary: Spartacus beat two consuls and marched north, perhaps hoping to leave Italy.

beats.scene: Rebels argue at the foot of snow-capped mountains, then turn their wagons south
beats.summary: For reasons that historians still debate, the rebels turned back south into Italy.

beats.scene: A wealthy general in a red cloak inspects ranks of tired soldiers
beats.summary: Rome gave the command to Crassus, the richest man in Rome, who restored discipline harshly.

beats.scene: A long ditch and wall cross a narrow peninsula as soldiers dig by torchlight
beats.summary: Crassus trapped the rebels in the toe of Italy, and pirates failed to carry them to Sicily.

beats.scene: A long road at dusk lined with crosses, and a lone traveller walking
beats.summary: Spartacus died in 71 BCE, and the revolt did not end slavery, but his name lived on.

beats.scene: Crowded apartment blocks stand beside rich villas, and a legion marches by
beats.summary: Conquest brought Rome wealth, but also poverty and bitter quarrels between rich and poor.

beats.scene: A general in armour at the gates of Rome with soldiers behind him
beats.summary: Generals found that loyal soldiers could win them power, and Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BCE.

beats.scene: A young man in a toga refuses an order from a stern dictator's officer
beats.summary: Julius Caesar, born in 100 BCE, refused the dictator Sulla and left Rome.

beats.scene: A young Roman in a toga sits calmly among rough pirates
beats.summary: Pirates captured the young Caesar, and he told them that he would have them punished.

beats.scene: Caesar speaks to a cheering crowd in the Forum
beats.summary: Back in Rome, Caesar won the crowd's love with shows and speeches, and he borrowed heavily.

beats.scene: Three men clasp hands over a table with a map of the known world
beats.summary: In 60 BCE Caesar, Pompey and Crassus made a private alliance, and Caesar became consul.

beats.scene: A general on horseback looks over a wide green land of rivers and forests
beats.summary: In 58 BCE Caesar took command in Gaul and began years of war.

beats.scene: Soldiers build a long wooden bridge across a wide river
beats.summary: He bridged the Rhine in about ten days and sailed to Britain twice, but did not conquer it.

beats.scene: Two rings of wooden walls surround a hill fort, with soldiers inside and out
beats.summary: In 52 BCE Caesar besieged the Gaulish leader Vercingetorix at Alesia and won the war.

beats.scene: A general reads sad news in his tent while a rider waits
beats.summary: Crassus and Caesar's daughter Julia died, and Pompey drifted away from Caesar.

beats.scene: Senators argue in a hall while one holds out a sealed letter
beats.summary: In 50 BCE the Senate, backed by Pompey, wanted Caesar to give up his army.

beats.scene: Caesar studies a map in a tent as his officers wait for orders
beats.summary: Caesar feared that his enemies would put him on trial if he came home as a private man.

beats.scene: Soldiers stand beside a small river at dawn, a general in front
beats.summary: In January 49 BCE Caesar led one legion to the little river Rubicon at the border of Italy.

beats.scene: Pompey and senators hurry out of Rome by torchlight along a dark road
beats.summary: Pompey and many senators fled, and Caesar took Italy in a few weeks.

beats.scene: Two armies clash on a hot plain in Greece, one far larger
beats.summary: In 48 BCE Caesar beat the larger army of Pompey at Pharsalus, in Greece.

beats.scene: A young queen in a palace talks with a Roman general
beats.summary: Pompey was killed in Egypt, and Caesar helped the young queen Cleopatra to win her throne.

beats.scene: Caesar rides through Rome in a golden chariot as crowds throw flowers
beats.summary: Caesar won the last battles and celebrated four great triumphs in 46 BCE.

beats.scene: Workmen carve a new calendar on a stone wall in the Forum
beats.summary: As dictator he gave Rome a new calendar and helped the poor and his old enemies.

beats.scene: A golden chair and a statue stand in a temple while worried senators watch
beats.summary: In 44 BCE Caesar became dictator for life, and some feared that he wanted to be king.

beats.scene: Senators surround a man in a toga on the steps of a hall
beats.summary: On 15 March 44 BCE, senators led by Brutus and Cassius killed Caesar.

beats.scene: A crowd murmurs in the Forum as senators hurry away from a hall
beats.summary: After the Ides the killers had no plan, and Rome was in turmoil.

beats.scene: Caesar's body lies on a platform in the Forum while a crowd weeps
beats.summary: At Caesar's funeral the crowd turned against the killers, and Brutus and Cassius left Rome.

beats.scene: An eighteen-year-old in a plain tunic reads a letter beside a harbour
beats.summary: Octavian, Caesar's great-nephew, learned in Greece that he was Caesar's heir.

beats.scene: A thin young man steps off a ship onto an Italian beach
beats.summary: He returned to Italy, took the name Caesar and paid Caesar's gifts to the people.

beats.scene: An old soldier and a young heir argue across a table
beats.summary: Antony, Caesar's old general, did not wish to treat the boy as an equal.

beats.scene: Three men sign a document in a room with maps on the walls
beats.summary: In 43 BCE Octavian, Antony and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate.

beats.scene: Lists of names are nailed up in the Forum as citizens read in fear
beats.summary: They posted lists of their enemies to be killed, and Cicero was one of the victims.

beats.scene: Two armies meet on a muddy plain in northern Greece
beats.summary: In 42 BCE Antony and Octavian beat Brutus and Cassius at Philippi, and both killers died.

beats.scene: A Roman general in Greek robes meets a queen on a golden barge
beats.summary: Antony took the East, fell in love with Cleopatra and lived in Egypt.

beats.scene: A calm young man studies a map beside his friend Agrippa and a fleet
beats.summary: Octavian ruled the West, built a strong fleet with Agrippa and said that Antony was a traitor.

beats.scene: Ships with bronze rams clash at sea near a rocky coast
beats.summary: Octavian's fleet under Agrippa beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE.

beats.scene: Two figures in a dim palace in Alexandria as soldiers approach
beats.summary: Antony and Cleopatra fled to Egypt and took their own lives in 30 BCE.

beats.scene: Soldiers lead carts of gold and grain through the gates of Alexandria
beats.summary: Egypt became a Roman province, and its treasure and grain made Rome wealthy.

beats.scene: A young man rides in a chariot through cheering streets in Rome
beats.summary: In 29 BCE Octavian celebrated three triumphs, and the long civil wars were over.

beats.scene: Senators in white togas bow to a calm man in a plain robe
beats.summary: In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, and he became the first emperor.

beats.scene: A calm man in a plain robe stands while senators sit around him
beats.summary: He kept the old offices and called himself the first citizen, but he held the real power.

beats.scene: Soldiers stand in ranks beside a fort on a frontier river
beats.summary: Augustus paid his soldiers himself and kept them on the frontiers, and the civil wars ended.

beats.scene: Builders put up marble walls on a street of old brick shops
beats.summary: He rebuilt Rome in marble, made a fire brigade and built roads and aqueducts.

beats.scene: Officials and clerks sort scrolls and tax records in a provincial office
beats.summary: The empire was run by governors, tax collectors and soldiers, and its main languages were Latin and Greek.

beats.scene: An old man lies in a quiet bedroom while a younger man stands by

B1B2: Rome stands on seven low hills beside the river Tiber, not far from the sea. Today it is a huge city, but it began as a very small place.
The Tiber was easy to cross near an island in the river, so roads from the north and the south met there. Traders brought salt from the coast along a track that was later called the Salt Road.

The first Romans lived in villages of round huts with roofs of straw, and each hill may have had its own village. They kept sheep and goats, grew grain and fetched their water from springs and from the river.
Romans liked to say that their ancestors came from Troy, a city that was destroyed in a great war. A hero called Aeneas escaped from the flames and sailed west with his son and a band of followers.
In the story, Aeneas landed in Italy and married the daughter of a local king. His family later founded a town in the hills called Alba Longa, and their kings ruled it for many generations.
Numitor was the rightful king of Alba Longa, but his younger brother Amulius wanted the crown for himself. Amulius took it by force and pushed Numitor aside.

To make sure that his niece Rhea Silvia would have no sons, Amulius made her a priestess of Vesta, who was forbidden to marry. But she gave birth to twin boys, and she said that their father was Mars, the god of war.
Amulius was furious and afraid, because the boys might one day take his throne. He ordered a servant to carry them to the river and leave them there to die.

The Tiber was in flood, and the servant did not dare to go closer than the edge of the water. He set the basket down and hurried away, and when the river fell back, the basket stuck in the mud beneath a fig tree.
A writer called Livy set the story down about seven hundred years after the events it describes. That is why historians call it a legend, and not a record of what truly happened.
A she-wolf who had come to drink at the river heard the babies crying. Instead of attacking them, she fed them with her milk, and a woodpecker is said to have brought them food as well.
Faustulus, a shepherd who looked after the king's animals, found the twins near the wolf's cave. He was amazed, and he took them home to his wife, who agreed to bring them up as her own sons.

The boys, who were named Romulus and Remus, grew up among the sheep, and they were strong, quick and fearless. They hunted wild animals and chased away robbers, and soon the young men of the hills looked to them as leaders.

After a quarrel with some herdsmen, Remus was captured and taken to the old man Numitor, who began to guess who he really was. When the truth came out, the brothers attacked Amulius, killed him and gave the throne back to their grandfather.
Rather than live in Alba Longa under their grandfather, the brothers wanted a city of their own. They chose the hills beside the Tiber, close to the place where the wolf had found them.
The twins could not agree where the city should stand, or which of them should be its king. They decided to let the gods choose, and each brother sat on a hill to watch the sky for birds.
Romulus took a plough pulled by two oxen and cut a deep line around the Palatine Hill. This furrow was a sacred boundary, and it showed exactly where the wall of the city would stand.

Remus laughed at the low wall and jumped over it to show how weak it was. In the best-known version of the story, Romulus killed his brother in a rage and warned that anyone else who crossed it would die.

Romulus became the first king, and he wanted his young city to grow quickly. The legend says that he welcomed runaways, poor men and exiles, but hardly any women were among them, which caused trouble with the neighbours.

Archaeologists have found the post holes of small huts on the Palatine Hill, which date from about the eighth century BCE. The date of 753 BCE was worked out much later by Roman scholars, and nobody can prove that Romulus ever lived.

According to tradition, Rome had seven kings in turn, from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud. Historians think that some of the stories are true and some are invented, and they cannot always tell which are which.
Numa Pompilius, the second king, was said to be a gentle man who loved peace more than war. He organised the priests and the festivals, and he is credited with arranging the first Roman calendar.
Tullus Hostilius, the third king, was as warlike as Numa had been peaceful. When Alba Longa broke its promises, he destroyed the town and brought its people to live in Rome.
According to tradition, Ancus Marcius, the fourth king, built the first wooden bridge across the Tiber. He is also said to have founded a port called Ostia, where the river meets the sea.

Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king, came from an Etruscan city to the north, where people were rich and skilled. Rome later copied many Etruscan customs, such as the purple-edged robe and the bundle of rods that was carried before an official.
Between the hills lay a marshy valley where water collected after every rain. The kings are said to have built a great stone drain, and the dry ground became a market place called the Forum.

Servius Tullius, the sixth king, was said to have been born to a slave woman before he rose to the throne. He counted all the citizens and sorted them by wealth, so that richer men served in the army with better weapons.
Tarquin the Proud, the last king, was said to be the grandson of the fifth king, and he took the throne by force. He did not ask the Senate for approval, and he punished anyone who opposed him.
Tarquin built a huge temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill, one of the largest in Italy. Many Romans were forced to work on it, and they did not forget how hard the work had been.

By now the nobles feared the king's anger, and ordinary people resented the heavy work that he forced them to do. More and more Romans began to say that one man with unlimited power was too dangerous.
In the legend, Sextus, the son of King Tarquin, attacked a noblewoman named Lucretia in her own home. She told her father and her husband Collatinus what had happened, and then she took her own life.

Lucius Junius Brutus was a relative of the king, and he had always pretended to be a fool so that he would be left alone. Now he threw off the pretence, held up the knife and made everyone swear to drive the Tarquins out of Rome.

The angry citizens gathered in the Forum, and the army outside the city turned against the king as well. When Tarquin hurried back to Rome, the gates were closed against him, and he was sent into exile, traditionally in 509 BCE.
Rome now elected two leaders called consuls, who held office for only one year. The first two were Brutus and Collatinus, and each of them could keep a close eye on the other.
Each consul could veto, or stop, whatever the other tried to do, so that no man could rule alone. The Romans came to hate the very word king, and for centuries even the strongest leaders avoided it.

Tarquin asked an Etruscan king named Porsena to help him win back the throne, and Porsena marched on Rome. In the legend, a soldier named Horatius held the wooden bridge alone while his friends chopped it down behind him.

Rome now called itself a republic, which comes from Latin words meaning a public thing. It was run by the Senate, a council of elders, and by assemblies of citizens, and its banners carried the letters SPQR.

In practice, a few rich patrician families held most of the power, and they filled the Senate and the high offices. The poorer plebeians had little say, and many of them fell into debt and could be forced to work for their creditors.

In 494 BCE, according to tradition, the plebeians refused to fight or work and walked out of the city. The rich needed them, so they agreed that the plebeians could elect officials called tribunes, who could protect any citizen from unfair treatment.

For years the plebeians complained that nobody knew what the law really said, because the nobles kept it to themselves. About 450 BCE, tradition says, the laws were cut on tablets called the Twelve Tables and set up in the Forum for everyone to read.
By about 400 BCE the Romans had defeated many of the towns around them, one after another. They did not always destroy their enemies, but made them into allies who had to send soldiers to Rome.

For years the Romans besieged Veii, a rich Etruscan city only a short march from their own. In 396 BCE, according to tradition, they finally captured it under a general named Camillus, and Rome gained its fertile land.

The Gauls were Celtic peoples who lived north of the Alps, in lands that are now France and beyond. They were farmers, metalworkers and fierce warriors, and Romans and Greeks both feared their tall fighters with long moustaches.

Some Gaulish tribes crossed the Alps in search of better land and settled in the valley of the river Po. From there they raided their neighbours, and in time one of their war bands marched south into central Italy.

A Gaulish army was besieging the Etruscan town of Clusium, and Rome sent three envoys to ask for peace. According to the story, the envoys broke the rules and joined the fighting, so the Gauls demanded that they be punished.

Rome refused to punish the envoys, and the angry Gaulish chief Brennus led his army straight towards the city. They marched so fast that the Romans had little time to gather an army or to call on their allies.
The two armies met beside a small river called the Allia, about eleven miles north of Rome. The Gauls charged with loud war cries, and the Roman line, which was badly placed, broke almost at once.

The Roman soldiers threw down their shields and fled in terror, and many of them swam across the Tiber. Some ran back into the city and up to the Capitoline Hill, and they were so frightened that they did not even close the gates.

The Romans knew that they could not defend the whole city, so most families left for nearby towns. The men who could fight, with the senators and priests, went up to the Capitoline Hill with all the food that they could carry.

According to the legend, some old men who were too weak to leave decided to stay and die in their robes. They sat silently on ivory chairs, and when a Gaul touched one man's beard, the old man struck him with his staff.

The Gauls entered Rome without a fight, and at first they were surprised to find the streets empty. They went from house to house, took whatever they wanted and killed the people who had stayed behind.

Soon afterwards the Gauls set fire to many houses, and Roman writers described the city as almost completely burned. Modern archaeologists have found some traces of burning, but not enough to show that the whole city was destroyed.

The defenders held the Capitoline Hill, a steep rock with only one easy path, and the Gauls could not capture it. The siege dragged on for months, and the legend says that it lasted for about seven months.

Food ran short on the hill, and the Gauls in the camps below were suffering from sickness and hunger as well. Meanwhile Camillus, who had been sent into exile, gathered a new army in a nearby town and waited for his chance.

One night the Gauls noticed signs that a Roman messenger had climbed the cliff in secret. They decided to use the same path, and a line of warriors began to climb up in the dark without making a sound.

The guards were asleep and the dogs did not bark, but the geese of the goddess Juno heard the Gauls and honked loudly. A soldier named Marcus Manlius woke up, ran to the edge and hurled the first climber down the slope.

The guards who had failed were punished, while Manlius was rewarded with gifts from the grateful soldiers. For centuries the Romans remembered the geese, and they carried out a yearly ceremony to honour them.

At last the Romans and the Gauls agreed that the Gauls would leave if they received a thousand pounds of gold. The legend says that the Romans complained about the weights, and Brennus then threw his sword onto the scale to make the price higher.

In the Roman version, Camillus arrived just in time, stopped the payment and drove the Gauls away in a great battle. A Greek historian named Polybius gave a more modest account, saying that the Gauls left because enemies were attacking their homes in the north.

After the Gauls had gone, the Romans rebuilt their houses in a great hurry, with narrow, crooked streets. They also built a long wall of stone around the seven hills, and for about eight hundred years no foreign enemy captured Rome again.
Carthage was a rich trading city on the coast of North Africa, in what is now Tunisia. Its merchants sailed all over the Mediterranean, and its navy was the strongest at sea.

By about 270 BCE Rome ruled most of Italy, not by keeping all the people down but by making them allies. Roman roads linked the towns together, and every ally had to send soldiers whenever Rome asked for them.

In 264 BCE Rome and Carthage began to fight over Sicily, which lay between them across a narrow sea. The Romans called the Carthaginians Poeni, which is why the three wars between the two cities are called the Punic Wars.

Rome was a land power with no navy, but it could not win in Sicily without ships. According to tradition, Roman carpenters copied a Carthaginian warship that had been wrecked, and soon the republic had a fleet.
The Romans were not yet good sailors, so they fixed a bridge with a spike to each ship. When an enemy came close, soldiers crossed onto its deck and fought as if on land.

After more than twenty years of war, the Romans won a great sea battle near the Aegates Islands in 241 BCE. Carthage gave up Sicily and agreed to pay a huge sum of silver, and Sicily became Rome's first province outside Italy.

Carthage was poorer and angry, and its great general Hamilcar Barca went to Spain to rebuild its strength. There he found mines of silver and good soldiers, and he founded a new base that would pay for another war.

According to the story, Hamilcar took his young son Hannibal to an altar and made him swear never to be a friend of Rome. Hannibal grew up among soldiers, and he was known later for his courage and his clever plans.

When Hamilcar died, other commanders led the Carthaginians in Spain, until Hannibal became the general at the age of twenty-six. In 219 BCE he laid siege to Saguntum, a Spanish city that was friendly to Rome, and he captured it after eight months.
Roman envoys went to Carthage, and one of them held up a fold of his toga to offer peace or war. The Carthaginians chose war, and the Second Punic War began in 218 BCE.

Hannibal decided that Rome could not be beaten at sea, so he chose to attack by land. He marched out of Spain with a very large army, which included thousands of horsemen and thirty-seven war elephants.

At the river Rhône, local tribes tried to stop the army, and the elephants had to cross the wide, fast water. According to ancient writers, Hannibal's men built rafts, covered them with earth to look like land and so ferried the frightened animals across.

The Alps were the hardest part of the march, because the paths were narrow and snow had already begun to fall. Landslides and attacks by mountain tribes killed many soldiers and animals, and no one today knows for certain which pass the army used.

Hannibal reached the plains of northern Italy with perhaps twenty-six thousand men, but he found that the local Gauls were willing to join him. He won his first two battles against the Romans, at the rivers Ticinus and Trebia, and the Romans were badly shaken.

In 217 BCE a Roman army marched along the shore of Lake Trasimene on a misty morning. Hannibal's men were hidden on the hills above, and they attacked from all sides so that thousands of Romans were killed or trapped.

Rome now chose a cautious leader named Fabius, who decided not to fight Hannibal in open battle. He followed the Carthaginians and cut off their supplies, and angry Romans gave him a nickname, the Delayer, which later became a title of honour.

In 216 BCE the Romans met Hannibal near the town of Cannae with a much larger army, and they were sure that they would win. Hannibal placed his weakest soldiers in the centre and let them step back, so that the Romans pushed forward into a trap.

After the horror of Cannae, many Romans feared that the city would fall, but the Senate refused to make peace. It raised new armies, even by enlisting slaves and young boys, and many allies in central Italy stayed loyal to Rome.

Rome sent a young general named Scipio to Spain, and later he carried the war across the sea to Africa itself. Hannibal was called home, and in 202 BCE the two generals met at the battle of Zama, where Scipio won.

Carthage had to give up its navy and its empire, but later Romans still feared it. One senator, Cato, kept saying that Carthage must be destroyed, and in 146 BCE the Romans took the city and burned it.
By the first century BCE, slavery was part of daily life in Rome, in houses, on farms and in mines. Some historians think that about one person in four in Italy was enslaved.

Most slaves had been taken as prisoners in Rome's wars, and others had been kidnapped by pirates or bought from foreign traders. Many more were simply born into slavery, because the child of a slave belonged to the master.

Great landowners kept huge numbers of slaves on their farms, and the work in the fields and mines was hard and often cruel. In the cities, however, some educated slaves became teachers, doctors, secretaries or managers, and a few earned enough to buy their freedom.

In law a slave was the master's property, and he or she could be bought, sold or punished at the master's wish. Some masters treated their slaves kindly and freed them after many years, while others were harsh, and the slave had almost no way to complain.

Many Romans lived with a quiet fear that the people they owned might one day fight back. Two large slave revolts had already shaken the island of Sicily, and the Senate had needed years and many soldiers to put them down.

The Romans did not invent fights between armed men, but they turned them into a famous entertainment. The first recorded gladiator fight in Rome was at a funeral in 264 BCE, paid for by the dead man's family.

Over time, rich men opened schools where slaves, prisoners and some volunteers learned to fight with swords, shields and nets. The crowds loved the contests, and school owners earned money by hiring out their men.

One of the men in the school at Capua was Spartacus, who came from Thrace, in the Balkans. According to the writer Plutarch, he had once served in the Roman army, but later he was captured, enslaved and sold to the school.

In 73 BCE about two hundred men in the school decided to escape, but someone betrayed the plan. About seventy of them heard the news in time, and they broke out of the kitchen with knives, spits and whatever else they could find.

On the road outside, the escaped men found a wagon full of gladiators' weapons and took it for themselves. They chose three leaders, Spartacus and two Gauls named Crixus and Oenomaus, and they made their camp on the slopes of Mount Vesuvius.
The Senate sent about three thousand soldiers under a commander named Glaber, who blocked the only easy path up the mountain. He thought that hunger would soon force the rebels to give in.

The rebels, however, were clever, and they twisted the strong wild vines that grew on the mountain into long ropes. They let themselves down the cliff behind the Roman camp, and they attacked the soldiers while they were still unprepared.

News of the victory spread across the countryside, and many slaves ran away from their masters to join Spartacus. Most of them were herdsmen and farm workers, who knew the land well and were used to hard physical work.

The rebels defeated several Roman forces, and they captured weapons, horses and standards that Roman soldiers were proud to carry. Ancient writers said that the rebel army grew to tens of thousands, although the exact number is uncertain.

The rebel leaders did not agree about what to do next, because some wanted to leave Italy and others wanted to stay and plunder. Crixus separated from Spartacus with a large group of followers, and a Roman army killed him in battle.

Spartacus defeated two consuls who tried to stop him, and then he led his followers north towards the Alps. Some historians think that he planned to cross the mountains and lead his people to their homelands, which would have meant freedom.

At the edge of northern Italy the rebels turned back south, and we do not know the reason. Perhaps the Alps seemed too dangerous, or perhaps many of his followers preferred plunder in Italy to a long march home.

By now the Senate was frightened, and it gave the command to Marcus Licinius Crassus, who was the richest man in Rome. He restored discipline in a hard way, and when one legion ran away, he ordered every tenth man to be killed.

Crassus trapped the rebels in the far south of Italy and ordered his men to dig a long ditch across the narrow land. Spartacus had made a deal with pirates who promised to carry his army to Sicily, but the pirates took the money and sailed away.

In 71 BCE Spartacus died fighting in the last battle, and about six thousand captured rebels were crucified along the road from Capua to Rome. Slavery went on for centuries, but the name of Spartacus was never forgotten.

As Rome conquered more land, a few families grew very rich from war, slaves and taxes, while many ordinary citizens lost their farms. The poor and the rich quarrelled bitterly, and the old rules of the republic began to break down.

General Marius had opened the army to poor men, and soldiers began to look to their general, not to the Senate, for pay and land. In 88 BCE a general named Sulla marched his army into Rome itself, which no Roman commander had done before.

Julius Caesar was born in 100 BCE into an old family that claimed to be descended from the goddess Venus. When the dictator Sulla ordered him to divorce his wife, he refused, and he had to leave Rome to keep himself safe.

While Caesar was sailing across the Aegean Sea as a young man, pirates captured him and demanded a ransom. He laughed at the low price, told them to ask for more and promised to punish them, which he later did.

Caesar returned to Rome and began a political career, and he soon became popular with ordinary people. He paid for splendid shows and spoke up for the poor, and he borrowed so much money that he was often in debt.

In 60 BCE Caesar made a private deal with two other powerful men, Pompey the general and Crassus the millionaire. Together they could control the Senate, and in 59 BCE Caesar became consul, with Pompey marrying his daughter Julia.

After his year as consul, Caesar chose to take command of an army, and he was given Gaul, a rich and unconquered land. In 58 BCE he began a war that would last for eight years, and he won glory, wealth and loyal soldiers.

In 55 BCE Caesar built a wooden bridge across the Rhine in about ten days, to show the German tribes the power of Rome. He also crossed the sea to Britain twice, although he did not stay, and his journeys made him famous.

In 52 BCE the Gauls united under a chief named Vercingetorix, who made a stand in the hill fort of Alesia. Caesar surrounded the fort with a wall, built a second wall to guard against attack from outside and finally won the war.

Caesar's alliance with Pompey and Crassus began to break when Julia died in 54 BCE. Crassus was killed in a disastrous war in 53 BCE, and Pompey slowly joined the Senate's side against his old friend.
The Senate feared Caesar's power and wanted him to give up his command in Gaul, and Pompey agreed. Caesar replied that he would only do it if Pompey did the same, and the Senate refused this offer.
While Caesar commanded an army, the law protected him, but once he became a private man, his enemies could take him to court. He feared ruin, so he decided not to give up his army.

On the night of 10 January 49 BCE, Caesar and a single legion reached the little river Rubicon, which marked the border of Italy. A general who crossed it with an army broke the law, and Caesar knew that crossing meant civil war.
Pompey and most of the senators left Rome in a panic, and soon afterwards they sailed away to Greece. Caesar marched through Italy, and in a few weeks the whole land was in his hands.
In 48 BCE the two armies met at Pharsalus in Greece, and Pompey had far more soldiers than Caesar. Caesar's veterans were more skilful, however, and they broke the enemy line and won a great victory.

Pompey sailed to Egypt, where the officials of the young king killed him, hoping to please Caesar. Caesar then stayed in Alexandria and helped the young queen Cleopatra, who wanted to rule Egypt without her brother.

Caesar spent the next three years fighting Pompey's supporters in Asia, Africa and Spain, and he won every time. In 46 BCE he returned to Rome and celebrated four triumphs, with crowds cheering him through the streets.

As dictator, Caesar gave Rome a new calendar of 365 days with an extra day every four years, and that calendar is the basis of ours. He also found land for his old soldiers and for the poor, and he spared many of his enemies.

In 44 BCE the Senate made Caesar dictator for life, and he accepted honours that no Roman had ever held before. His enemies whispered that he wanted to become a king, even though he had refused a crown at a public festival.
On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, about sixty senators plotted to kill Caesar. They surrounded him at a meeting of the Senate, and he fell at the foot of a statue of his old rival Pompey.

After the Ides of March, the killers walked out into the Forum, but the people stayed silent and many ran home. The conspirators had no plan for governing Rome, and Caesar's friend Mark Antony was the other consul.

At Caesar's funeral in the Forum, Antony spoke to the crowd and read out the will, which left money to every citizen. The crowd grew angry, and Brutus and Cassius were soon in danger, so they left Rome and went east.

Caesar's great-nephew Octavian was only eighteen, and he was studying in Greece when his mother wrote to him. The will named him Caesar's adopted son and heir, which was a huge inheritance for a young man.

Octavian hurried home to Italy, and he decided to take the name Caesar, even though his friends advised against it. Caesar had left gifts of money to the people of Rome, and the young man sold his own property to pay them.

Antony had been Caesar's general, and he thought that he should lead the Caesarian party. He treated the young heir as a boy at first, but Octavian had Caesar's name and the loyalty of many of Caesar's veterans.

Antony and Octavian quarrelled and almost fought, but they needed each other against Caesar's killers. In 43 BCE they joined with a third man, Lepidus, and they formed a group of three that is called the Second Triumvirate.

The three men wanted to destroy their enemies, so they posted lists of names in the Forum. Those on the list could be killed, and ancient writers say that hundreds of senators died, including the great speaker Cicero.
In 42 BCE Antony and Octavian led an army to northern Greece and met Brutus and Cassius at Philippi. After two battles the two killers had lost, and both of them took their own lives.

After Philippi the Triumvirs divided the Roman world between them, and Antony took the rich lands of the East. There he met Cleopatra, the queen of Egypt, and he stayed with her for years, and he began to live in the Greek style.
Octavian took charge of the West, where his friend Agrippa built a strong fleet and defeated Sextus Pompey. Octavian told the Romans that Antony had betrayed Rome for a foreign queen.

In 31 BCE the two fleets met near Actium, on the western coast of Greece. Agrippa's ships were smaller and faster, so Antony and Cleopatra were beaten, though the two leaders escaped with a few ships.
Antony and Cleopatra fled to Egypt, and Octavian followed them with his army the next year. Antony took his own life, and Cleopatra died soon afterwards.
Octavian made Egypt a province of Rome, and he took its royal treasure and its rich harvests. The money paid his soldiers, and the grain of Egypt helped to feed the city for the next centuries.

In 29 BCE Octavian returned to Rome and celebrated three triumphs over three days. After nearly twenty years of civil war, the Romans were tired of fighting, and they welcomed the man who promised them peace.

In 27 BCE Octavian offered to give up his powers, but the senators begged him to stay and gave him the name Augustus. The name means something like revered, and from this moment historians call him the first Roman emperor.

Augustus knew that Romans hated kings, so he kept the old offices and called himself the first citizen. He sat in the Senate as an ordinary senator, but he controlled the army, the money and the provinces.

Augustus kept a permanent army and paid his soldiers himself, which made them loyal to him and not to a general. He placed most of the legions on the frontiers, and in 9 CE three legions were lost in Germany, so the Rhine became the border.

Augustus is said to have boasted that he found Rome built of brick and left it built of marble. He also built roads and aqueducts, and he started a fire brigade for the city, and he added to the Forum with a new temple.

The empire was run by governors in the provinces, who collected taxes and kept order with the help of the army. Latin was the language of government in the West, while Greek stayed in use in the East.
Augustus ruled for more than forty years and died in 14 CE at the age of seventy-five. His stepson Tiberius took his place, and the Romans found that the empire could continue without its founder.

In 79 CE the Bay of Naples was one of the loveliest and busiest places in the empire, with fishing boats, rich villas and farms. Above it rose a green mountain called Vesuvius, which looked as peaceful as any hill in Italy.

Pompeii was a lively town near the bay, and probably ten or twelve thousand people lived there. It had been Roman for more than a century and a half, but many people still spoke the old local language as well as Latin.
The forum was the heart of Pompeii, a wide open space with temples, law courts and a large market. People came here to trade, to talk politics and to meet their friends.

Many houses in Pompeii had no kitchens, so people bought hot food at counters in the street, called thermopolia. The town also had dozens of bakeries, with stone mills and ovens, where bread was baked for the whole city.

Rich families lived in large houses built around a courtyard, with painted walls, mosaic floors and a garden. Poorer people rented small rooms over the shops, and slaves slept wherever there was space.

The amphitheatre in Pompeii could hold thousands of spectators, who came to watch gladiators fight. In 59 CE fans from Pompeii and the nearby town of Nuceria fought there, and Rome banned games in Pompeii for a time.

In 62 CE a strong earthquake damaged the town, and walls and buildings fell down. Seventeen years later, workers were still repairing some of the damage, so nobody could have said that the town was in danger.
Vesuvius did not look like a volcano, because its slopes were covered with vineyards and farms. It had been quiet for centuries, and the Romans had no word for what was inside it.
Herculaneum was a smaller seaside town, a few miles from Pompeii, and many rich families had villas there. It lay close to the mountain, and its position made it even more dangerous than Pompeii.
In the days before the eruption, the ground shook a little from time to time. Earthquakes were common in that part of Italy, so few people were worried by them.

The eruption began around midday, when Pliny the Younger was seventeen years old and staying with his uncle near Naples. His mother pointed out a cloud of unusual size and shape, like a tall pine tree, which was rising from the mountain.

Pliny the Elder commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum, and he was also a famous scholar who had written a huge book about nature. He was curious about the cloud, so he ordered a fast boat to take him closer.

Before the boat left, a messenger brought a note from a woman named Rectina, who lived at the mountain's foot and begged for help. Pliny changed his plan and ordered warships to sail across the bay and rescue people from the coast.

As the ships crossed the bay, ash began to fall on them, hot and thick, followed by pieces of pumice and burned stones. The helmsman told Pliny to turn back, but the admiral ordered him to sail on towards Stabiae.

They landed at the house of a friend in Stabiae, and Pliny tried to calm everyone by eating dinner and then going to bed. During the night, however, the courtyard filled with ash and stones, and the building began to shake.

They feared that the roof would fall in, but they also feared the stones falling outside, so they tied pillows to their heads for protection. They went out into the dark, with torches, and the sea was too rough to leave by ship.
At Pompeii, light grey stones called pumice fell for many hours and piled up in the streets. The weight made roofs collapse, and many people ran from the town, taking what they could carry.

The next morning, a cloud of burning ash and gas rushed down the mountain at great speed and swept through the nearby towns. Anyone who had stayed in Pompeii or Herculaneum was killed, because no one could survive the heat.

Pliny the Elder lay down on the beach at Stabiae, and later he died, probably because he could not breathe the poisoned air. His nephew wrote about the day in a letter to the historian Tacitus, and it is the only eyewitness account that we have.

The new emperor Titus sent officials to help the survivors, but the towns were never rebuilt, and people forgot where they had been. Workers began to dig them out in the eighteenth century, and now they show us Roman daily life, while Rome carried on.

A Roman citizen had three names, like Gaius Julius Caesar, and these showed his personal name, his clan and his family. For many people, being a citizen was a matter of great pride, and it was worth more than money.

Citizens could vote in the assemblies, serve in the legions, make contracts under Roman law and appeal against unfair judgements. They were also protected from some of the harshest punishments, which were used freely on slaves and foreigners.

Rome's allies in Italy fought in its armies, but they were not citizens, and they did not have a voice in its decisions. In 91 BCE they began a war, called the Social War, because they wanted the same rights as Romans.

The Romans won the war, but they also realised that they could not simply defeat their neighbours for ever. They gave citizenship to the Italian allies, and within a few years almost all free men in Italy were citizens.
Rome also brought in new citizens through the gift of freedom, since a freed slave of a citizen usually became a citizen. His children would have full rights, which was unusual among ancient peoples.

Roman soldiers from the provinces served in units called the auxiliaries, and they were not citizens when they joined. After about twenty-five years of service they received a bronze certificate that made them citizens, and for a time their children too.

The emperor Claudius was born in Gaul, and he argued that Rome had always grown stronger by welcoming outsiders. In 48 CE he let rich Gauls enter the Senate, and a bronze tablet with his speech was found in Lyon.

Under the emperor Trajan, the empire stretched from Britain in the north to the Persian Gulf in the east. In 117 CE it reached its greatest size, though some of the new lands in the east were given up soon afterwards.

The next emperor, Hadrian, decided that Rome should protect its borders and not try to grow forever. He travelled across the provinces and began a long wall in northern Britain in 122 CE, and parts of it can still be seen.

Merchants, soldiers and farmers lived in towns from Syria to Spain, and they spoke Latin, Greek, Celtic and many other languages. Most of them were not citizens, so they had fewer rights than those who were.

Septimius Severus, who came from North Africa, became emperor in 193 CE, and after his death in 211 CE his sons ruled together. The elder son, Caracalla, was named after a type of Gaulish cloak, and he soon had his brother Geta killed.
In 212 CE Caracalla issued a decree that made almost all free people in the empire Roman citizens. It was one of the most important laws in Roman history, and it affected millions of people.

People have long asked why Caracalla did it, and a Roman historian named Cassius Dio said that the emperor wanted more money. Citizens had to pay certain taxes, so the number of tax payers would rise.

A part of the decree survives on a scrap of papyrus found in Egypt, now kept in the German city of Giessen. Caracalla's full name was Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, and many of the new citizens took the name Aurelius in his honour.

The decree did not include slaves, who remained the property of their owners. It also left out some peoples who had surrendered to Rome, but most free people in the empire now had the same legal status.

Before the decree, being Roman had meant belonging to the city of Rome or, at least, to Italy. Now it meant having a legal status, and a farmer in Egypt or a merchant in Britain could be just as Roman as a senator.

In practice the law still favoured the rich, whose punishments were lighter and who were more likely to win in court. So the decree gave people more rights on paper, but citizenship no longer felt as special as it had before.

In 235 CE the empire entered a dark period that historians call the third-century crisis. Armies fought each other, invaders crossed the frontiers, a plague spread, and the emperors made their coins worse by mixing in cheap metal.

In about fifty years more than twenty men were named emperor, and most of them were murdered or killed in battle. Each new ruler had to buy the loyalty of his soldiers, and the soldiers could remove him whenever they chose.

The Persians captured an emperor, and the empire split into three parts, with its own rulers in Gaul and in the East. The emperor Aurelian finally won them back, and in the 270s he built a great wall around the city of Rome.

The empire had grown so large that one emperor could hardly rule it, so in 284 Diocletian shared power with three other rulers. Each of the four kept an army and guarded a part of the empire, and Diocletian himself retired in 305.

Constantine became sole emperor in 324, and he decided to build a new capital in the east. He chose the old Greek city of Byzantium on the Bosporus, which was easy to defend, and in 330 CE he renamed it Constantinople.

When the emperor Theodosius died in 395, he left the empire to his two sons, one in the east and the other in the west. After this the two halves never again had one ruler, and the eastern half grew richer than the western half.

A people called the Huns rode out of the steppes of Asia and pushed many Germanic tribes towards the Roman frontier. In 376 a large group of Goths asked permission to cross the Danube and settle in the empire, and the emperor agreed.

The Goths were treated badly by Roman officials, and soon they rebelled and began to plunder the Balkans. At Adrianople in 378, they destroyed the Roman army and killed the emperor Valens, who was fighting in the front line.

The Rhine was supposed to protect the western empire, but according to tradition, it froze on the last night of 406. Vandals and other tribes walked across the ice into Gaul, and the Romans could not stop them.

The Visigoths, under their king Alaric, marched into Italy, and in 410 CE they entered Rome through a gate that was opened at night. They plundered the city for three days, and it was the first time in eight hundred years that an enemy had taken it.

The news of the sack spread all over the Roman world, and many people were deeply shocked. Some blamed the new religion for angering the old gods, and a bishop in North Africa named Augustine wrote a long book in reply.

The empire was short of money and soldiers, so it pulled its troops out of the far provinces. Traditionally about 410 CE, the legions left Britain, and the emperor told the British cities to look after themselves.

In 451 Attila, the king of the Huns, invaded Gaul, and the next year he invaded Italy. In 455 the Vandals from North Africa plundered Rome for two weeks, and western emperors were now often weak men chosen by generals.

By 475 the real power in the west belonged to the generals, who were often of German origin. One of them, Orestes, made his young son the emperor, and the boy was named Romulus, though people called him Augustulus, which means little Augustus.

Most of the army in Italy was made up of German soldiers, who wanted land to settle on. They asked for a third of the land of Italy, and Orestes refused, because he did not want to give so much to them.
The soldiers rebelled, and they chose an officer named Odoacer as their leader. Odoacer defeated Orestes in the summer of 476 and had him killed, and the boy emperor was now alone.

Odoacer removed the young emperor from his throne in 476 CE, but he spared him and gave him a pension. The boy lived in a villa in southern Italy, and nobody knows for certain what happened to him afterwards.

Odoacer sent the crown and purple robes to the eastern emperor Zeno, and he said that Italy no longer needed an emperor of its own. He went on to rule Italy as a king, and Zeno accepted this, since he had other problems.

Hardly anyone at the time believed that the Roman Empire had come to an end. Farmers still brought their goods to market, the Senate still met, and Italy was soon ruled by another king, Theodoric the Ostrogoth.

The eastern half of the empire lasted for nearly a thousand years more, and its people always called themselves Romans. Today we call it the Byzantine Empire, and it fell only in 1453, when the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople.
Historians still argue about why the western empire fell. Some point to invasions and civil wars, others to weak money, plague and a government that had become too big to manage.

Rome's gifts to the world were many, and Latin turned into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian. Roman law, roads and concrete buildings, such as the great dome of the Pantheon, are also part of its legacy.
The letters SPQR are still stamped on manhole covers in Rome, and Caesar's name lives on in words such as Kaiser and tsar. Rome's story began with a basket on a river, and it never really ended.
C1C2: The city of Rome sits on a bend of the river Tiber, among a cluster of low hills that the Romans later counted as seven. Its empire once reached from Britain to the deserts of the Middle East, and it shaped the world that came after it. Yet every great story has a beginning, and the beginning of Rome was small, muddy and surrounded by questions that nobody can fully answer.

Near an island in the Tiber, the river could be crossed by a shallow ford, and so travellers going north or south found themselves passing through the same spot. Merchants carried salt from the coast along a track that was later named the Salt Road, and they paused to trade at the foot of the hills. A place that others must pass through is a place that can grow rich, and Rome was fortunate in its position.

Long before marble temples rose above the valleys, the people of the hills lived in round huts with thatched roofs, and they farmed the land around them. They kept sheep and goats, ploughed small fields of grain and probably quarrelled over pasture, as neighbours often do. Each hilltop was a little community with its own habits, and only later did these communities join together under a single name.

Long afterwards, the Romans liked to trace their descent from Troy, the city that the Greeks were said to have destroyed after a ten-year war. According to the story, a Trojan nobleman named Aeneas escaped from the flames, carrying his old father on his back, and sailed west in search of a new home. Nobody can say whether any such man lived, but the tale gave Rome an ancient and noble ancestry that rivalled the Greeks' own.

In the legend, Aeneas landed on the coast of Italy, married the daughter of a local king and became the ancestor of a long line of rulers. His descendants founded a town named Alba Longa in the hills southeast of the Tiber, and their kings sat on the throne for many generations. The Romans later claimed that Rome itself was only a daughter of Alba Longa, born when two of its princes went looking for a place of their own.

Numitor was the rightful king of Alba Longa, but his younger brother Amulius was ambitious and ruthless, and he seized the throne by force. Numitor was pushed aside, his son was killed, and the old man was left to live quietly in the countryside. Amulius had one more worry, however, which was that his niece might one day bear a son who would demand the crown back.

To make certain that Numitor would have no grandsons, Amulius forced his niece Rhea Silvia to become a priestess of the goddess Vesta, a role that forbade her to marry. Yet the story says that she gave birth to twin boys, and that she named Mars, the god of war, as their father. The Romans, who loved to link their city with divine power, were proud of this claim, and they repeated it for centuries.

When the king learned of the babies, he was both furious and frightened, for he knew that two grown sons of a royal house could easily become rivals. He ordered a servant to carry the twins to the Tiber and abandon them, so that the river would commit a crime that he did not dare to commit with his own hands. The servant, however, was a man of conscience, and he could not bring himself to do exactly what he had been told.

The Tiber had burst its banks that season, and the frightened servant dared go no farther than the edge of the flood, where he set down the basket and hurried away. As the waters sank, the basket came to rest in the mud at the foot of a fig tree, and the two babies lay there crying in the wild, hungry and alone. The Romans later pointed out a particular fig tree near the Palatine Hill, and they honoured it for centuries as the very tree of the story.

The oldest tale we can read in full detail was told by Livy, a historian who lived more than seven hundred years after the date that the Romans gave for the founding. By then the story had been polished by generations of poets, speakers and storytellers, and nobody could check it against any written record. Historians therefore treat it as a legend, which is valuable for what it shows about the Romans' beliefs, though not as a reliable account of what really happened.

The twins might have died there, but a she-wolf that had come down to the river to drink heard their cries and came over to them. In the story she did not harm them; she fed them with her milk and licked them clean, while a woodpecker, another creature sacred to Mars, brought scraps of food. The Romans never tired of this picture, and the wolf with two babies became the emblem of their city.

Soon afterwards a shepherd named Faustulus, who tended the royal flocks nearby, saw the wolf slip away and found the two healthy babies lying where she had left them. He was astonished, but he was also a kind man, and he carried them back to his hut, where his wife agreed to raise them as their own. The couple called the boys Romulus and Remus, and they gave them the same plain upbringing as any shepherd's sons.

The twins grew up among the flocks, learning to herd, to hunt and to fight, and they were soon known for their strength and their courage. They chased off thieves and wild animals, shared whatever they won with the other young shepherds, and gathered a loyal band of friends around them. Even so, nobody on the hills guessed that these two bold young men were the grandsons of a king.

One day, after a quarrel with the herdsmen of Numitor, Remus was captured and brought before the old man, who looked into his face and began to wonder who he really was. Faustulus then told the whole story of the basket, the river and the wolf, and the brothers gathered their friends and marched on Alba Longa. They killed the cruel Amulius and gave the throne back to their grandfather, and with that justice done, the twins turned their minds to a new ambition.

Having restored their grandfather, the twins had no wish to stay in Alba Longa as the junior members of someone else's household, and they longed to build a city of their own. They chose the hills beside the Tiber, the very ground where they had been saved as babies and where they had spent their youth among the flocks. The place was easy to defend and close to the river, and it seemed to them that the gods had marked it out long before.

Since both brothers wanted to rule, they agreed to let the gods decide, and each sat on a separate hill to watch the sky for a sign. Remus saw six vultures first, but then Romulus saw twelve, and each brother claimed that the gods had favoured him. The Romans believed deeply in such omens, called auspices, and they continued to read the flight of birds before major decisions for many centuries.

Romulus then harnessed a bull and a cow to a plough with a bronze blade and cut a deep furrow around the Palatine Hill, to mark the line of the future wall. The Romans regarded this line as sacred, and in later centuries they performed a similar ceremony whenever they founded a new colony. Within it stood the safe, holy ground of the city, and beyond it lay the world of strangers and danger.

Remus, still bitter about the vultures, mocked the low wall that his brother had begun to build, and he leaped over it to show how easily an enemy could do the same. In the best-known version of the tale, Romulus struck him down in a fit of rage and declared that anyone else who jumped the wall would suffer the same fate. Other versions say that Remus died in a brawl between the two sets of followers, and the Romans themselves admitted that their city began with a killing.

Now alone, Romulus became the first king, and he opened his city as a refuge for runaways, outlaws and landless men from all over the neighbouring country. The legend says that this crowd of newcomers lacked wives, and that the Romans therefore invited their Sabine neighbours to a festival and carried off their young women by force. After a war that followed, the Sabines and the Romans made peace, and the old story presents this as the origin of the Roman people.

Archaeologists working on the Palatine Hill have uncovered the post holes of small round huts from around the eighth century BCE, which fits the legend better than anyone expected. The date of 753 BCE, however, was calculated much later by Roman scholars, and no evidence proves that a king named Romulus ever lived. Whatever the truth, the Romans cherished the story, and it shaped how they saw themselves for the next thousand years.

By Roman tradition, seven kings ruled the city in turn between 753 and 509 BCE, from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud. That would give each king an average reign of about thirty-five years, which makes modern historians suspicious, and they doubt many of the names, dates and deeds. Even so, the later Romans believed that the kings had shaped their laws, their religion and their buildings, and the stories show what they thought was important.

The second king, Numa Pompilius, was remembered as a gentle and thoughtful ruler who preferred prayer to war. He was said to have organised the priests, the sacred fires and the festivals, and he was credited with an early calendar in which January and February were added to the old ten months. Later Romans pointed to his long, quiet reign as proof that a state needs religion as well as soldiers.

Tullus Hostilius, the third king, was as warlike as Numa had been peaceful, and he spent much of his reign fighting the neighbours of Rome. In the legend, a war with Alba Longa was decided by a duel between three Roman brothers, the Horatii, and three Alban brothers, the Curiatii, and the Romans won the contest. When Alba later broke its promises, Tullus destroyed the town and brought its people to live on the Caelian Hill, and Rome grew stronger by taking in the people it had beaten.

According to tradition, Ancus Marcius, the fourth king, built the first wooden bridge across the Tiber, which linked the city to the land on the other bank. He is also said to have founded Ostia, a port at the mouth of the river, so that Rome could reach the sea and the salt works nearby. Archaeologists believe that Ostia may be somewhat younger than the legend says, but the idea that Rome needed a harbour is certainly an old one.

Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king, came from an Etruscan city to the north, where the people were wealthy, skilled in metalwork and proud of their ancient culture. The Romans later told how many of their own customs had come from the Etruscans, among them the purple-edged robe, the carved chair of office and the bundle of rods that was carried in front of a magistrate. Historians think that Etruscan kings or leaders really did rule in Rome for a time, so this part of the legend may rest on solid ground.

Between the hills lay a marshy valley where water gathered after every rain and made it useless for building. The kings, according to tradition, solved the problem by digging a great stone drain, the Cloaca Maxima, parts of which still survive beneath the modern city. Once the ground was dry, it became a market place and meeting ground called the Forum, and for a thousand years it remained the heart of Roman public life.

Servius Tullius, the sixth king, was said to have been born to a slave woman before he rose to the throne, and the story made him a hero of humble people.
