He ordered a count of all citizens and sorted them into classes by wealth, so that richer men served in the army with better weapons and had a greater say in the assemblies. Later Romans also credited him with building the first great wall around the hills, although the wall that survives today was built much later.

Tarquin the Proud, the last king, was said to have taken the throne by force after Servius was murdered, and he never asked the Senate for its approval. He ruled through fear, punishing his enemies, putting some nobles to death and surrounding himself with guards, which was something earlier kings had not needed. The Romans remembered him as a tyrant, and the word for king became one of the worst insults in their language.

Tarquin built a huge temple to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva on the Capitoline Hill, and it was said to be one of the largest in Italy. He is said to have forced ordinary citizens to carry stone and dig foundations, a burden that increased their bitterness against him. The temple was traditionally dedicated in 509 BCE, the very year in which the king was driven out, and it remained the greatest shrine of Roman power for centuries.

By the end of his reign the nobles feared the king's anger, and ordinary people resented the heavy work he demanded from them. More and more Romans whispered that one man with unlimited power was too dangerous, and that no family should be allowed to hold the city for itself. All that was needed was a spark, and the legend supplies one in the shocking story of a noblewoman named Lucretia.

In the legend, Sextus, the son of King Tarquin, attacked a noblewoman named Lucretia in her own home, and she sent for her father and her husband Collatinus. After she had told them what had happened, and had made them promise to take vengeance, she took her own life in front of them. The ancient writers who told this story wanted to show how the royal family had insulted the honour of Roman households, and historians cannot say how much of it is true.

Lucius Junius Brutus was a relative of the king, and he had survived the royal family's cruelty by pretending to be slow-witted, which is why his name means something like dull. At Lucretia's side he threw off the pretence, raised the knife that had caused her death and made everyone present swear to drive the Tarquins out of Rome. The Romans admired him for this, and for centuries they held him up as a model of the citizen who puts his country before his family.

The angry citizens gathered in the Forum, and the army camped outside the city sided with Brutus as well. When Tarquin hurried back to Rome to restore order, he found the gates closed against him, and he was sent into exile with his family, traditionally in 509 BCE. Historians suspect that the real change was slower and less dramatic than the legend suggests, but the Romans always dated their freedom from that year.

Rome now elected two leaders called consuls, who held office for only one year and shared the power between them. The first two were Brutus and Collatinus, though Collatinus soon lost his place because he belonged to the Tarquin family, and the story shows how suspicious the Romans had become. The yearly election gave the city a simple rule that lasted for centuries, which was that no man should hold supreme power for long.

Each consul had the right to veto, or stop, whatever the other tried to do, so that no man could rule alone. The Romans came to hate the very word king, and for centuries even the strongest leaders took care to avoid it, preferring other titles that sounded humble and traditional. Many years later, when one man did gather all the power in his hands, he was careful to say that he was only the first citizen.

Tarquin appealed to an Etruscan king named Porsena, who marched on Rome with an army and nearly took the city. In the legend, a soldier named Horatius held the wooden bridge across the Tiber alone while his friends chopped it down behind him, and then he plunged into the river in his armour and swam to safety. A few ancient writers hint that Porsena may even have captured Rome for a time, which the proud Roman story naturally left out.

Rome now called itself a republic, from Latin words meaning a public thing, because in theory the state belonged to all its citizens rather than to a family. It was run by the Senate, a council of elders made up mostly of men who had held high office, and by assemblies in which citizens voted on laws and elections. The letters SPQR, standing for the Senate and People of Rome, appeared on its banners, its coins and its public buildings, and they are still seen in the city today.

In practice, a handful of rich patrician families held most of the power, and they filled the Senate and the highest offices year after year. The poorer plebeians had very little say, and many of them fell into debt, which in the early republic could force them to work for their creditors as if they were slaves. A republic that gave all the benefits to a few was bound to be unstable, and the Romans spent the next two centuries arguing about how to share them.

In 494 BCE, according to tradition, the plebeians refused to fight or work and marched out of the city, which left the rich without soldiers, farmers or craftsmen. The nobles needed them, so they agreed that the plebeians could elect officials called tribunes, who had the power to protect any citizen from unfair treatment and to veto the acts of magistrates. It was the first great victory of ordinary Romans, and it set a pattern in which the poor won a little more power each time they threatened to walk away.

For years the plebeians complained that nobody knew what the law actually said, because the nobles kept it to themselves and explained it as they pleased. About 450 BCE, according to tradition, a board of ten men wrote down the main rules on tablets called the Twelve Tables, and these were set up in the Forum for anyone to read. The Roman Republic changed slowly, step by step, and by the end of the following century plebeians could hold every office, even the consulship, although in reality the old families kept much of their influence.

By about 400 BCE the Romans had defeated many of the towns around them, one after another, and the republic had become the leading power in central Italy. They did not always destroy their enemies, preferring to turn them into allies who sent soldiers to Rome whenever it asked. This habit of making friends out of the conquered, rather than killing them all, was one of the secrets of Rome's later success.

For years the Romans besieged Veii, a rich Etruscan city only a short march from their own, and the long struggle was said to have lasted ten years, like the war at Troy. In 396 BCE, according to tradition, they finally captured it under a general named Camillus, and Rome gained a great stretch of fertile farmland. The victory almost doubled the city's territory, and it made the Romans confident that nothing could stop them.

The Gauls were a group of Celtic peoples who lived north of the Alps, in lands that are now France and the countries around it. They were farmers, metalworkers and fierce warriors, and both Romans and Greeks feared the sight of their tall fighters with long moustaches, shining necklaces and painted shields. Their society was divided into many tribes, and each chieftain won his place by leading his followers to wealth and glory.

Some Gaulish tribes crossed the Alps in search of richer land, and over a few generations they settled in the broad valley of the river Po, in northern Italy. The Etruscans, who had lived there before, lost much of their territory, and from the new settlements the Gauls raided and bargained with the peoples further south. Eventually, one of their war bands marched towards central Italy, and Rome found itself in the way.

A Gaulish army was besieging the Etruscan town of Clusium, and Rome, which had made friends with the Etruscans, sent three envoys to ask for peace. According to the story, the envoys broke the rules of diplomacy by joining the fighting, and one of them killed a Gaulish chief with his own hand. The Gauls demanded that the guilty men be handed over, but the Romans, instead of punishing them, elected them to high office, and the outraged Gauls turned their army towards Rome.

Brennus, the Gaulish leader, led his army straight along the road to the south, and he moved so fast that Rome had very little time to prepare. The Romans gathered every soldier they could find, but their forces were hastily collected and had never faced warriors like these. It was a dangerous moment for a young republic, and the next few days would test everything that Rome had built.

The two armies met beside a small river called the Allia, about eleven miles north of Rome, on a day that the Romans later marked as one of the unluckiest of the year. The Gauls charged with terrifying war cries and the blare of their war horns, and the Roman line, which was too long and badly placed, broke almost at once. Whatever the exact date was, historians usually place the battle about 390 BCE, although some ancient writers give a slightly different year.

The Roman soldiers threw down their shields and fled in terror, and many of them swam across the Tiber, which carried some of them to safety and drowned others. Thousands escaped to Veii, which was now in Roman hands, while the rest ran back to the city and up to the Capitoline Hill, so panicked that they did not even stop to close the gates. The Gauls, astonished at their own victory, are said to have paused for a day before they dared to approach the empty walls.

The Romans knew that they could not defend the whole city, so most families left for nearby towns, taking what they could carry. The men who could fight, together with senators, priests and supplies of food, went up to the Capitoline Hill, the only place that seemed possible to defend. A plebeian named Lucius Albinus is said to have given up his cart to carry the Vestal priestesses and the sacred objects of the city, so that they, at least, would be safe.

According to the legend, a number of old men who were too weak to leave decided to stay and die in their robes, since they had already served their country. They sat silently outside their houses on their ivory chairs, and when a Gaul reached out and touched the beard of one of them, the old man struck him with his staff. The Romans loved this story, for it showed the dignity and stubbornness of their ancestors, and whether or not it is true, it shows how they wished to be remembered.

The Gauls marched into Rome through gates that were wide open, and at first they were uneasy, suspecting some kind of trap in the silent, empty streets. When no trap appeared, they went from house to house, took whatever they wanted and killed the people who had stayed behind. For the first time in its history, the city of the seven hills was in the hands of a foreign army.

Soon afterwards the Gauls set fire to many houses, and Roman writers later described the city as almost completely burned to the ground. Modern archaeologists have found some traces of burning from about this time, but not enough to show that every part of the city was destroyed, and it is possible that the Romans exaggerated the disaster. Still, the memory of the fire was powerful, and it taught the Romans to see the Gauls as a standing danger that could return.

The defenders held the Capitoline Hill, a steep rock with only one easy path up its slope, and the Gauls found that they could not capture it by force. The siege dragged on for months, and the legend says that it lasted about seven months, long enough for the besiegers to grow weary and discontented. On the hill itself, the Romans suffered from hunger, but they were determined not to give in.

Food ran short on the hill, and the Gauls in their camps below were also suffering from sickness and hunger, because they had settled in the ruins of a hot city in the middle of summer. Meanwhile Camillus, the hero of Veii, who had been sent into exile before the war, gathered a new army in a nearby town and waited for his chance. The legend says that a brave young man swam the Tiber and climbed the cliff in the night to ask the Senate to name Camillus dictator, which they did.

One night the Gauls noticed signs on the rock that the messenger had climbed the cliff in secret, such as broken plants and scraped stones. They decided to use the same path, and a line of warriors began to climb up in the dark, silently passing their weapons from hand to hand. They had almost reached the top without any alarm, and Rome was within a few moments of falling.

The guards were asleep and even the dogs did not bark, but the geese of the goddess Juno, which had been kept in her temple and were nearly starved, heard the Gauls and honked loudly. A soldier named Marcus Manlius woke up, grabbed his weapons, ran to the edge of the cliff and hurled the first climber down the slope, knocking the men behind him over like a row of stones. The alarm spread, the defenders rushed to the cliff, and the attack failed, thanks to a flock of geese.

The guards who had slept at their posts were punished, while Manlius was rewarded with gifts of food and wine from the grateful soldiers. For centuries the Romans remembered the geese that saved their city, and they carried out a yearly ceremony to honour them, which was a remarkable tribute to a bird usually found in farmyards. The story has been told so often that it has become a symbol of the way small, unexpected helpers can save a nation.

At last the Romans and the Gauls agreed that the Gauls would leave if they received a thousand pounds of gold, a vast sum for the besieged and weary city. The legend says that the Romans complained that the Gauls were using false weights, and Brennus then threw his sword onto the scale to make the price higher, mocking them for their weakness. The story was told in Rome for centuries as a lesson in the bitterness of defeat, though some Romans claimed that the ransom was never paid at all.

In the Roman version, Camillus arrived just in time, stopped the payment and drove the Gauls away in a great battle, so that the city was saved by the sword rather than bought with gold. A Greek historian named Polybius, who lived later and had no reason to flatter Rome, gave a more modest account, saying that the Gauls left because enemies were attacking their homes in the north. We cannot be sure which version is right, but the Romans clearly preferred to remember a victory over a bargain.

After the Gauls had gone, the Romans rebuilt their houses in a great hurry, which is why, later writers said, the streets of Rome were narrow and crooked. They also built a long wall of stone around the seven hills, and the shock of the disaster made them resolve never again to be caught unprepared. For about eight hundred years no foreign enemy captured Rome, until the Visigoths finally broke in during the year 410 CE.

Carthage was a rich trading city on the coast of North Africa, in what is now Tunisia, and its merchants sailed to every part of the Mediterranean. Founded long before by Phoenician settlers, it had a powerful navy, a wealthy council and a ring of colonies in Spain, Sicily and Sardinia. For many years Rome and Carthage had been friends, but as both grew stronger, it became harder for both to share the sea.

By about 270 BCE Rome ruled most of Italy, not by keeping all its conquered neighbours down, but by making them allies who owed it soldiers and loyalty. Roman roads, built to carry armies quickly, linked the towns together, and a citizen of a distant Italian town could feel that he belonged to a great alliance. This network would soon be tested to the limit, for the Romans were about to fight the strongest naval power of the age.

In 264 BCE the Romans and the Carthaginians began to quarrel over the island of Sicily, which lay between them across a narrow strait. The Romans called the Carthaginians Poeni, because the city had been founded by Phoenicians, and from this word we get the name of the Punic Wars, the three great struggles between the two cities. Neither side had planned a long conflict, but this first war lasted for more than twenty years.

Rome was a land power with no navy, and it could not win in Sicily without ships, so the senators decided to build a fleet from nothing. According to tradition, Roman carpenters copied a Carthaginian warship that had been wrecked on the coast, while crews practised rowing on dry land before they ever set out to sea. A hundred ships or more were ready within a few months, and the Carthaginians were astonished.

The Romans knew that they could not match the skill of Carthaginian captains, so they invented a clever trick for sea battles. They fixed a heavy boarding bridge with a spike to the front of each ship, so that when an enemy ship came close, the bridge crashed down and held it fast, and the Roman soldiers rushed across. A fight at sea became a fight on land, which was just what the Romans wanted.

After more than twenty years of war, and after the loss of many fleets in storms, the Romans won a great sea battle near the Aegates Islands in 241 BCE. Carthage gave up Sicily and agreed to pay a huge sum of silver over many years, and Sicily became Rome's first province outside the mainland of Italy. Soon afterwards, while Carthage was fighting its own rebellious soldiers, Rome also seized the islands of Sardinia and Corsica, which left an anger that Carthaginians never forgot.

Carthage was poorer and angry, and its great general Hamilcar Barca went to Spain to rebuild the strength of his country. There he found rich silver mines, good soldiers and many tribes eager to make agreements, and he founded a new base that would pay for another war. He was determined that his city would one day take its revenge, and he brought up his sons to share that purpose.

According to the story, which Hannibal himself was said to have told many years later, his father took him as a boy of about nine to an altar and made him swear never to be a friend of Rome. We cannot know how much of this is true, but there is no doubt that Hannibal grew up among soldiers, learned the art of war from his father and was known for his courage and his cunning. Roman writers, even when they hated him, admitted that he was one of the greatest commanders of the ancient world.

When Hamilcar died, other men led the Carthaginian forces in Spain, until in 221 BCE the army chose Hannibal as its general at the age of only twenty-six. Two years later he laid siege to Saguntum, a Spanish city that had friendly ties with Rome, and he captured it after about eight months, in spite of Roman protests. Rome saw this as an act of war, and the Senate sent envoys to Carthage to demand an answer.

Roman envoys went to the Carthaginian council and demanded that Hannibal be handed over for what he had done at Saguntum. The story says that the leader of the envoys held up a fold of his toga and said that he carried peace and war inside it. When the Carthaginians told him to choose for himself, he shook out war, and they accepted it, so that the Second Punic War began in 218 BCE, and it became the most dangerous war Rome ever fought.

Hannibal decided that Rome could not be beaten at sea, since the Romans now had the stronger navy, so he chose to attack by land. He left some troops to guard Spain and marched out with a large army, which included thousands of horsemen and thirty-seven war elephants, to take his enemy by surprise in Italy. It was one of the boldest plans in history, and the Romans, who expected the war to be fought in Spain and Africa, were not ready.

At the river Rhône, local tribes tried to stop the army, and the elephants had to cross the wide, fast water, which they hated. According to ancient writers, Hannibal's men built rafts, covered them with earth so that the animals would think that they were walking on solid ground, and ferried them across one by one. The Romans sent a fleet to find him, but he had already moved on, and by the time they arrived, he was marching towards the mountains.

The Alps were the hardest part of the march, because the paths were narrow and steep, and snow had already begun to fall in the high passes. Landslides, ambushes by mountain tribes and bitter cold killed many soldiers and animals, and one Roman writer claimed that Hannibal broke up rocks by heating them with fire and pouring vinegar over them, a story that many historians doubt. No one today knows for certain which pass the army used, and scholars still argue about the route.

Hannibal reached the plains of northern Italy with perhaps twenty-six thousand men, thin, tired and with only a few elephants left alive, but he found that many of the local Gauls were glad to join him against Rome. He won his first two battles against the Romans, at the rivers Ticinus and Trebia, the second in winter snow, and the republic was badly shaken. The Romans learned that this was an enemy with a brilliant mind, and that no ordinary tactics would be enough.

In 217 BCE a Roman army marched along the shore of Lake Trasimene on a misty morning, with no idea that the enemy was near. Hannibal's men lay hidden on the hills above, and they poured down on every side, trapping the Romans between the slopes and the water, so that thousands were killed and many more taken prisoner. The disaster, which came only a few months after the battle at the Trebia, convinced many in Rome that a new approach was urgently needed.

Rome now chose a cautious leader named Fabius, who decided that the best way to defeat Hannibal was not to fight him in open battle. He followed the Carthaginians, cut off their supplies and attacked small groups, all without risking a full contest, and angry Romans gave him the nickname of the Delayer, which was meant as an insult. Years later, when more daring plans had failed, they came to see that his slow and patient method was the only one that worked, and the name became a title of honour.

In 216 BCE the Romans met Hannibal near the town of Cannae with the largest army that they had ever put into the field, and most of them were sure that they would win. Hannibal placed his weakest soldiers in the centre and let them step back slowly, so that the Romans pushed forward into the curve, while his best infantry and horsemen closed around them from the sides and from behind. By the end of the day, tens of thousands of Romans had been killed or captured, and it was one of the worst defeats in the history of Rome.

After the horror of Cannae, many Romans feared that the city would fall, yet the Senate refused to make peace, and it even refused to pay a ransom for the prisoners. It raised new armies by enlisting slaves and boys, and although some allies in the south went over to Hannibal, the loyalty of most of central Italy held firm. The war went on for years, and Hannibal, who never had enough men or siege machines to attack Rome itself, stayed in southern Italy hoping that the republic would crack.

Rome sent a young general named Scipio to Spain, where he defeated the Carthaginians one by one, and later he carried the war across the sea to Africa itself. Hannibal was called home to defend his city, and in 202 BCE the two generals met at the battle of Zama, where Scipio won a decisive victory. Hannibal later went into exile, and when the Romans came to seize him, he is said to have taken poison rather than be captured.

Carthage was forced to give up its navy and its overseas empire, but later Romans still feared it, and one senator named Cato is said to have ended every speech by demanding that Carthage must be destroyed. In 146 BCE, after a third war, the Romans took the city after a long siege, burned it and sold the survivors into slavery, although the tale that they sowed the fields with salt is probably a later invention. Rome had now become the undisputed master of the western Mediterranean, and the whole sea would soon be known as its own.

By the first century BCE, slavery had become part of daily life in Rome, as it was in almost every ancient society. Slaves cooked and cleaned in the houses of the rich, ploughed the great estates and dug in the mines, and some historians estimate that about one person in four in Italy was enslaved. The wealth and comfort of the republic depended on this work, and few Romans, even among the kindest, thought of questioning it.

Most slaves had been taken as prisoners in Rome's wars, and each victory in Greece, Spain or Africa sent thousands of new captives to the markets. Others had been kidnapped by pirates and sold, or bought from foreign traders, and a great many were simply born into slavery, since the child of a slave belonged to the master. The Romans did not choose slaves by race, and a person who was free one year might lose everything in a war the next.

Great landowners kept hundreds of slaves on their estates, and the work in the fields and mines was exhausting and often cruel, with workers sometimes chained at night. In the cities, however, the position could be very different, for some educated Greek slaves became tutors, doctors, secretaries or managers, and a few earned enough to buy their freedom. The range between these two extremes was enormous, and it is a mistake to think that every slave in Rome lived the same life.

In law a slave was the master's property, who could be bought, sold, hired out or punished at his owner's wish, and who could not own anything or marry under Roman law. Some masters treated their slaves with kindness and freed them after years of service, and a freed slave could become a citizen, while others were harsh and violent, and the slave had almost no way to complain. It was a system founded on power, and the powerless had very little protection against abuse.

Many Romans lived with a quiet fear that the people whom they owned might one day turn against them, and the stories of earlier revolts were still fresh. Two large slave rebellions had already shaken the island of Sicily, and the Senate had needed years and many soldiers to put them down, which showed how dangerous such a rising could become. This history of fear made the Romans suspicious, and it also made them quick to punish.

The Romans did not invent fights between armed men, but they turned them into one of the most famous entertainments of the ancient world. The first recorded gladiator fight in Rome took place in 264 BCE, at the funeral of a nobleman whose sons paid for three pairs of men to fight in his honour. In the following centuries, the contests grew bigger and more splendid, until crowds of thousands came to watch them in great stone arenas.

Over time, wealthy men opened schools where slaves, prisoners and a few volunteers learned to fight with swords, shields and nets, and the school at Capua was one of the best known. The crowds loved the contests, and the owners of the schools earned good money by hiring out their men to politicians and families who wanted to put on a show. The fighters were fed well and trained hard, but they were also locked up, guarded and treated as things to be used.

One of the men at Capua was Spartacus, a Thracian from the Balkans, who was said to be both strong and unusually intelligent. According to the Greek writer Plutarch, he had once served in the Roman army and later been captured, enslaved and sold to the school, where his wife, a Thracian prophetess, is said to have shared his fate. Spartacus was not the only gifted man in the school, but he became the one whose name the world remembers.

In 73 BCE about two hundred men in the school decided to escape, but the plan was betrayed, and the group acted before it could be stopped. About seventy of them broke out of the kitchen with knives, spits and whatever else they could lay their hands on, and they fought their way through the streets of Capua. It was a small beginning for a revolt, and the escape was nearly all luck and courage.

On the road outside the town, the escaped men found a wagon full of gladiators' weapons, which was on its way to another school, and took it for themselves. They chose three leaders, Spartacus and two Gauls named Crixus and Oenomaus, and withdrew to the slopes of Mount Vesuvius, where they could defend themselves and see their enemies coming. The mountain was a volcano, but it had been quiet for so long that few people thought of it as dangerous.

The Senate did not take this small band seriously, and it sent about three thousand hastily collected soldiers under a commander named Glaber to put them down. Glaber blocked the only easy path to the summit and waited, believing that hunger would soon force the rebels to give in. The Romans had never expected that a band of slaves would be able to outwit them.

The rebels, however, were resourceful, and they twisted the strong wild vines that grew on the mountain into long ropes and let themselves down the steep cliff behind the Roman camp. They attacked at a moment when the soldiers were not expecting a fight, and they overran the camp, taking weapons, armour and horses. It was a brilliant stroke, and it showed the Romans that Spartacus was not a common bandit but a leader with a gift for strategy.

News of the victory spread across the countryside, and slaves began to leave their masters to join Spartacus, as well as poor free workers who had nothing to lose. Most of them were herdsmen and farm workers, who knew the land well, were used to hard work and could use their strength with great effect. The small band of fugitives was soon becoming an army, and a very dangerous one, because it had Roman weapons and local knowledge.

The rebels defeated several Roman forces and captured weapons, horses and even the standards that Roman soldiers were proud to carry, so that many Romans felt shame as well as fear. Ancient writers said that the rebel army grew to tens of thousands, and some give much higher figures, although such numbers are probably exaggerated. Spartacus was training these men carefully, and he used the same tactics that Roman armies used themselves.

The rebel leaders did not agree about what to do next, because some wanted to leave Italy and others preferred to stay and plunder the rich estates. Crixus separated from Spartacus with a large group of followers, and a Roman army killed him in battle, which was a heavy loss. Spartacus then held funeral games for him, and, in a cruel reversal, he made Roman prisoners fight as gladiators, as slaves had once been made to fight for Rome.

Spartacus defeated two consuls who tried to stop him, and then he led his followers north towards the Alps, a long way from the Roman heartland. Some historians believe that he planned to cross the mountains and lead his people back to their homelands in Thrace and Gaul, which would have meant real freedom. If this was his aim, it was a sensible one, and the Romans, who had expected a march on Rome, were surprised to see him leave.

At the edge of northern Italy the rebels turned back south, and the ancient writers do not explain exactly why, so historians must guess. Perhaps the Alps seemed too dangerous, or perhaps most of his followers preferred to plunder the rich towns of Italy than to make a long journey into unknown territory. It was a fatal decision, since it gave Rome the time it needed to find a general who could finish the job.

By now the Senate was truly frightened, and it gave the command to Marcus Licinius Crassus, who was the richest man in Rome and an ambitious politician. He restored discipline in a harsh way, and when one legion ran away from a fight, he ordered every tenth man to be killed, a punishment that had not been used for generations. His soldiers feared him more than they feared the rebels, and that was exactly what he intended.

Crassus trapped the rebels in the far south of Italy and ordered his men to dig a long ditch and build a wall across the narrow land. Spartacus had made a deal with pirates who promised to carry his army to Sicily, where he hoped to raise a new revolt, but the pirates took the money and sailed away. The rebels were now caught between the sea and the Roman legions, and their only hope was to break through the wall.

In 71 BCE the rebels made one last attack, and Spartacus died fighting at the head of his men, although his body was never found. About six thousand captured rebels were crucified along the road from Capua to Rome, a terrible warning to anyone who thought of imitating them, and the Roman state moved on. Slavery continued for many centuries, so the revolt achieved nothing in practice, but the name of Spartacus has stayed alive ever since as a symbol of the wish for freedom.

As Rome conquered more land, a few families grew enormously rich from war, slaves and taxes, while many ordinary citizens lost their farms and drifted into the city. The poor and the rich quarrelled bitterly, and the old rules of the republic, which had been designed for a small city, began to break down under the weight of an empire. Ambitious men saw that the quickest way to power was to win the support of the people, or of the army.

The general Marius had opened the army to poor men with no land, and these soldiers began to look to their general, rather than to the Senate, for pay and for a farm when they retired. In 88 BCE a rival general named Sulla marched his army into Rome itself, which no Roman commander had ever done, and later he made himself dictator and killed many of his enemies. The precedent was fatal to the republic, for once one general had used his legions against the city, others could follow.

Julius Caesar was born in 100 BCE into an old patrician family that claimed to be descended from the goddess Venus, through Aeneas's son. When the dictator Sulla ordered the young man to divorce his wife, who was a relative of Sulla's enemies, Caesar refused, and he had to leave Rome and hide until friends persuaded the dictator to forgive him. It was an early sign that he was brave, stubborn and unwilling to be pushed around.

While Caesar was sailing across the Aegean Sea as a young man, pirates captured him and demanded a ransom. The story says that he laughed at the low price, told them to ask for more, joked with them while he waited and promised that he would come back and have them punished, which he later did. Whether every detail is true, the tale shows the sort of man the Romans remembered: calm, charming and perfectly sure of himself.

Caesar returned to Rome and began a political career, and he soon became popular with ordinary people, who admired his easy manner and generous nature. He paid for splendid shows, repaired the great Appian Way and spoke up for the poor, and he borrowed so much money to do this that he was often deep in debt. Rich supporters, and those who feared his enemies, were glad to lend him more.

In 60 BCE Caesar made a private deal with two other powerful men, Pompey, the great general, and Crassus, the millionaire who had crushed Spartacus. Together they could control the Senate, and the arrangement, which historians call the First Triumvirate, was never an official body, but it worked so well that in 59 BCE Caesar became consul, and Pompey married his daughter Julia. The three men had little in common except ambition, and the alliance depended on their continuing to need each other.

After his year as consul, Caesar chose to take command of an army rather than stay in Rome, and he was given Gaul, a rich land that was still largely unconquered. In 58 BCE he began a war that would last for eight years, and he won glory, enormous wealth and the devoted loyalty of his soldiers. His excuse was to protect Rome's allies from migrating tribes, but he also wanted a fortune and a great reputation.

In 55 BCE Caesar built a strong wooden bridge across the Rhine in about ten days, to show the German tribes the speed and power of Roman engineers. He also crossed the sea to Britain twice, although he did not stay, and his journeys made him famous, since few Romans had ever heard of the island. He wrote his own account of the war in simple, clear Latin, and it was read in Rome as he intended, which kept his name before the voters.

In 52 BCE the Gauls united for the first time under a young chief named Vercingetorix, who made a stand in the hill fort of Alesia. Caesar surrounded the fort with a ring of walls, built a second ring to guard against the Gauls outside, and defeated both armies. Vercingetorix surrendered, and Gaul became part of the Roman world, though ancient writers claimed that a million people died, a figure that is certainly exaggerated.

Caesar's alliance with Pompey and Crassus began to break in the years after the Gaulish war began, for events took away the ties that held the three men together. Julia died in 54 BCE, which removed the personal bond between her husband and her father, and Crassus was killed in 53 BCE in a disastrous war against the Parthians. Pompey slowly drifted toward the Senate, which feared Caesar's growing fame, and he began to see his old partner as a rival and a danger.

The Senate feared Caesar's power and wanted him to give up his command in Gaul, and Pompey, who had once been his friend, agreed. Caesar replied that he would only do so if Pompey did the same, but the Senate refused this offer and ordered him to disband his army. The deadlock could not be broken by words, and both men knew that one of them would have to give way.

As long as Caesar held an army and an official post, the law protected him, but as soon as he became a private citizen, his enemies could take him to court. He feared that he would be ruined, perhaps even exiled, and he decided that he would not give up his army, which was the source of all his power. His soldiers, who had won so much under him, were willing to follow wherever he led.

On the night of 10 January 49 BCE, Caesar and a single legion reached the little river Rubicon, which marked the border between Gaul and Italy. A general who crossed it with an army broke the law, and Caesar knew that this meant civil war and perhaps the end of the republic. The river itself was small, a mere stream in the hills, but its meaning was enormous.

The soldiers waded across the Rubicon and went on towards Rome, and later writers said that Caesar had spoken of the dice being thrown, though we cannot be sure of his words. Pompey and most of the senators panicked and left Rome, and soon afterwards they sailed away to Greece, thinking that they could raise a bigger army there. Caesar marched through Italy, and in a few weeks the whole land was in his hands.

In 48 BCE the two armies met at Pharsalus in Greece, and Pompey had many more soldiers than Caesar and the better cavalry. Caesar's veterans, however, were more skilful and more determined, and they broke the enemy line and won a great victory in a single day. Pompey escaped from the battlefield and fled to Egypt, hoping for a safe place where he could gather his forces again.

The officials of the young king of Egypt killed Pompey as he landed, hoping to please Caesar, who was following him. Caesar was shocked, and he stayed in Alexandria, where he took the side of the young queen Cleopatra, who wanted to rule Egypt without her brother. After a hard struggle in the city, Cleopatra became queen, and she bore a son whom she said was Caesar's.

Caesar spent the next few years fighting Pompey's supporters in Asia, Africa and Spain, and he won every time, sometimes in a few days, as the story goes. In 46 BCE he returned to Rome and celebrated four triumphs, for Gaul, Egypt, Pontus and Africa, with crowds cheering him through the streets. His old enemy Vercingetorix, who had been held prisoner for six years, was led in chains before the crowds and put to death.

As dictator, Caesar gave Rome a new calendar of 365 days with an extra day every fourth year, and that calendar, with small changes, is the basis of ours. He also found land for his old soldiers and for the poor, gave citizenship to many provincial people and spared many of his enemies, which became famous as his clemency. These policies made him popular, but they also showed that one man was now making the decisions that the Senate once made.

In 44 BCE the Senate made Caesar dictator for life, and he accepted honours that no Roman had ever held before, including a golden chair and a statue in a temple. His enemies whispered that he wanted to become a king, even though he had publicly refused a crown at a festival, and many senators resented losing their old freedom. The old fear of kings, which the Romans had held for nearly five hundred years, was stirring once again.

On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, about sixty senators joined a plot to kill Caesar, led by Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius. They surrounded him at a meeting of the Senate, which was held in a hall beside the theatre built by Pompey, and he fell at the foot of a statue of his old rival. The conspirators believed that they were saving the republic, but they did not have any plan for what would come next.

After the Ides of March, the killers walked out into the Forum calling for liberty, but the people stayed silent and many ran home in fear. The conspirators had no plan for governing Rome, and Caesar's friend and fellow consul Mark Antony was able to take control of the situation. Within a few days the city was full of rumours and the soldiers of Caesar were on the move.

At Caesar's funeral in the Forum, Antony spoke to the crowd and read out the will, which left money to every citizen and gave Caesar's gardens to the public. The people, who had loved Caesar, grew angry and rioted, and Brutus and Cassius soon realised that they were in danger, so they left Rome and went east. The men who thought that they had saved the republic had become exiles, hunted by the heirs of the man whom they had killed.

Caesar's great-nephew Octavian was only eighteen years old, and he was studying in Greece when his mother wrote to tell him that his great-uncle was dead. The will named him as Caesar's adopted son and chief heir, which was a huge inheritance for a young man, and it brought him both great wealth and great danger. His friends warned him to refuse, but the boy, though frail and often ill, had a will of iron.

Octavian hurried home to Italy, and he decided to take the name Caesar, even though his friends advised against it, because the name was worth more than any army. Caesar had left gifts of money to the people of Rome, and when Antony refused to hand over the funds, the young man sold his own property to pay them. This generosity made him popular with the people, and it brought many of Caesar's soldiers to his side.

Antony had been Caesar's right hand in Gaul and in the wars that followed, and he believed that he should lead the Caesarian party. He treated the young heir as a boy at first, but Octavian had Caesar's name, his money and the loyalty of many of Caesar's veterans, and the two men quickly became rivals. The senator Cicero, who hated Antony, made speeches against him and tried to use the young man for the Senate's cause.

Antony and Octavian quarrelled and almost fought, but they found that they needed each other to face Caesar's killers, who had gathered armies in the East. In 43 BCE they joined with a third man, Lepidus, and the Senate gave them the power to rule for five years, which created a group of three that historians call the Second Triumvirate. Unlike the first alliance, it was official, and it gave the three men almost unlimited power.

The three men wanted to destroy their enemies, so they posted lists of names in the Forum and declared that anyone on the lists could be killed and that their property would be seized. Ancient writers say that hundreds of senators and thousands of others died, including the great speaker Cicero, who had spoken against Antony and was killed as he tried to escape. It was a time of terror, and the memory of it still stains Octavian's name.

In 42 BCE Antony and Octavian led an army across the sea to northern Greece and met the forces of Brutus and Cassius at Philippi. After two battles the killers of Caesar had lost, and both of them took their own lives rather than be captured, which ended the hopes of those who wished to save the old republic. The victory made Antony the most famous soldier in the Roman world, though Octavian had played a smaller part.

After Philippi the Triumvirs divided the Roman world between them, and Antony took the rich lands of the East, where he hoped to raise money and plan a war against the Parthians. There he met Cleopatra, the clever queen of Egypt, and he stayed with her for years, adopting Greek dress and customs, and the two had children and grand dreams. In Rome it was said that he had forgotten his country and was ruled by a foreign woman.

Octavian took charge of the West and faced the difficult task of finding land for thousands of soldiers, which made him unpopular in Italy. His loyal friend and general Agrippa built a powerful fleet and defeated Sextus Pompey, the son of Pompey the Great, who had been controlling the seas, and soon afterwards Lepidus was pushed aside. Octavian also told the Romans that Antony had betrayed them, and he made good use of every rumour about Cleopatra and her court.

In 31 BCE the two fleets met near Actium, on the western coast of Greece, in the most famous naval battle in Roman history. Agrippa's ships were smaller and faster than those of Antony and Cleopatra, and the fleet of the lovers was beaten, and the two leaders escaped with a few ships, while the rest of the army surrendered. The battle ended the last great struggle for power in the Roman world, and nobody was left who could challenge Octavian.

Antony and Cleopatra fled to Egypt, and Octavian followed them with his army the next year, and when they saw that all was lost, they took their own lives. Antony died first, and Cleopatra followed soon afterwards, and an old story says that she was bitten by a poisonous snake, though no one knows how she really died. With her died the last of the Greek kings and queens who had ruled Egypt for three centuries.

Octavian made Egypt a province of Rome, and he took its royal treasure and its rich harvests for the benefit of the Roman people. The money paid his soldiers and settled them on farmland, and the grain of Egypt would help to feed the city of Rome for centuries, so the province was ruled as his own property. Rome was now richer than ever before, and Octavian was the master of its wealth.

In 29 BCE Octavian returned to Rome and celebrated three triumphs over three days, for his victories in the north, at Actium and in Egypt. After nearly twenty years of civil war, the Romans were tired of fighting, and they were ready to welcome the man who promised them peace, order and an end to the killing. The temple of Janus, whose doors were open in time of war, was closed to show that peace had come.

In 27 BCE Octavian told the Senate that he would give up his powers and restore the republic, but the senators begged him to stay and gave him the name Augustus. The name means something like revered, and it carried religious weight without sounding like the title of a king, and from this moment historians call him the first Roman emperor. It was a clever arrangement, which left the shape of the republic in place while moving the real decisions to one man.

Augustus knew that the Romans hated kings, so he kept the old offices and the old forms and called himself the first citizen, which in Latin is princeps. He sat in the Senate as an ordinary senator, and he lived in a modest house, but he controlled the army, the money and the provinces, and so nobody doubted who held the real power. Many Romans were happy with this bargain, because they wanted peace more than they wanted the old politics.

Augustus kept a permanent army of about twenty-eight legions and paid his soldiers himself, which made them loyal to him and not to their generals. He placed most of the legions on the frontiers, far from Rome, and when three legions were destroyed in the forests of Germany in 9 CE, he was grief-stricken, and the Rhine became the northern border of the empire. For the first time, Rome had a standing army that could defend a great empire without threatening the capital.

Augustus is said to have boasted that he found Rome built of brick and left it built of marble, and the saying is a fair summary of his work. He built temples and a new forum, repaired roads, added aqueducts to supply the city with water and created a fire brigade and a police force to keep order. The city had grown to about a million inhabitants, and for the first time it began to look like the capital of a great empire.

The empire was run by governors in the provinces, who collected taxes, judged cases and kept order with the help of the army, and in return the provinces enjoyed peace and the protection of Roman law. Latin was the language of government in the West, while Greek remained the language of culture and trade in the East, and good roads and an imperial postal service linked the two halves. This system worked well enough that it lasted for centuries, with only small changes.

Augustus ruled for more than forty years and died in 14 CE at the age of seventy-five, having seen Rome change from a republic torn by civil war into a peaceful empire. His stepson Tiberius took his place, and the Romans discovered that the empire could continue without its founder, which proved that the new system was stable. Augustus had begun a long period of general peace, called the Pax Romana, that would last for about two centuries.

In 79 CE the Bay of Naples was one of the loveliest and busiest places in the Roman world, crowded with fishing boats, rich villas and prosperous farms. Wealthy Romans came here to escape the noise of the capital, and the sea breeze, the warm sunlight and the fertile soil made life easy. Above the bay rose a green mountain called Vesuvius, which looked as peaceful as any hill in Italy.

Pompeii was a lively town near the bay, and probably ten or twelve thousand people lived there, though nobody knows the exact figure. It had become Roman more than a century and a half before, but many people still spoke the old local language as well as Latin, and old inscriptions in the local language can still be read on some walls. Its merchants, craftsmen and farmers made a good living from the fertile land and the busy harbour.

The forum was the heart of Pompeii, a wide open space surrounded by temples, law courts, offices and a large market where farmers sold their produce. People came here to trade, to talk politics, to hear the news and to meet their friends, much as they do in the main squares of Italian towns today. Statues of the town's rich benefactors and of the emperors stood along the sides, and the whole place hummed with business.

Many houses in Pompeii had no kitchens, so people bought hot food at counters in the street, called thermopolia, which served stews, wine and bread from large pots set into the stone. The town also had dozens of bakeries, with stone mills turned by donkeys and big brick ovens, where bread was baked every morning for the whole community. Archaeologists have even found loaves of bread that were left in an oven on the final day.

Rich families lived in large houses built around a courtyard, with painted walls, mosaic floors, fountains and a garden at the back, and the artists who decorated them were skilled. Poorer people rented small rooms over the shops or lived in crowded apartments, and slaves slept wherever there was space, often in the kitchen or beside the stable. The differences between the rich and the poor were as great in Pompeii as in any city of the empire.

The amphitheatre in Pompeii, one of the oldest in the Roman world, could hold thousands of spectators, who came to watch gladiators fight. In 59 CE a riot broke out in the stands between fans from Pompeii and fans from the nearby town of Nuceria, and many people were killed or hurt, so Rome banned games in Pompeii for ten years. The Senate later allowed them again, which shows how much the people loved their entertainments.

In 62 CE a strong earthquake damaged the town, and walls, temples and houses fell down, and many people left to live elsewhere. Seventeen years later, builders were still repairing some of the damage, and nobody could have guessed that the real danger was still to come. The Romans did not connect these tremors with the mountain, because they did not know that it could erupt.

Vesuvius did not look like a volcano, because its slopes were covered with vineyards, farms and thick woods all the way to the top, and the famous wine of the region came from them. It had been quiet for centuries, perhaps even for hundreds of years, and the Romans had no word for what was hidden inside the mountain. A Greek geographer, Strabo, had noticed that the summit looked burned, but he guessed no more than that.

Herculaneum was a smaller seaside town, a few miles from Pompeii, and many rich families had built villas there with beautiful views of the bay. It lay closer to the mountain than Pompeii and on the side where the eruption would be fiercest, which made its position even more dangerous than that of its neighbour. Its houses, decorated with fine paintings and statues, were soon to be preserved in a strange and terrible way.

In the days before the eruption, the ground shook a little from time to time. Earthquakes were common in that part of Italy, however, and few people were worried by them, since they had been living with such tremors all their lives. Historians disagree about the date of the eruption, which tradition places on 24 August, though some recent discoveries hint at a date in the autumn.

The eruption began around midday, when Pliny the Younger, who was seventeen years old, was staying with his uncle at Misenum, on the northern side of the bay. His mother pointed out a cloud of unusual size and shape that was rising from the mountain, like a tall pine tree with a trunk and spreading branches, and it kept growing as they watched. He later described the sight in a letter, and so we know exactly what an eyewitness saw.

Pliny the Elder was the commander of the Roman fleet at Misenum, and he was also a famous scholar who had written a huge encyclopedia of nature, in thirty-seven books. He was curious about the cloud, and he ordered a fast boat to be prepared, so that he could take a closer look at the strange event as a scientist. It was the kind of choice that someone with his curiosity could hardly resist, but it would cost him his life.

Before the boat left, a messenger arrived with a note from a woman named Rectina, who lived at the foot of the mountain, and who begged for help because the only escape was by sea. Pliny changed his plan at once, and instead of going out as an observer, he ordered warships to sail across the bay and rescue the people from the coast. He had decided that he should act as a Roman commander, not merely as a scholar.

As the ships crossed the bay, ash began to fall on them, hot and thick, followed by pieces of pumice and burned black stones, and the sea suddenly grew shallow in front of them. The helmsman advised Pliny to turn back, but the admiral, who was not a man to retreat, ordered him to sail on towards Stabiae, where a friend of his lived. The night was growing dark, and the glow from the mountain lit the sky like a vast torch.

They landed at the house of a friend in Stabiae, and Pliny tried to calm everyone by eating dinner cheerfully and then going to bed, where he slept so deeply that people heard him snoring. During the night, however, the courtyard filled with ash and stones, and the building began to shake, so that his friends had to wake him before the door was blocked. The danger was greater than he had admitted, and the whole household faced a hard choice.

They feared that the roof would collapse, but they also feared the stones falling outside, so they tied pillows to their heads for protection, and went out into the dark carrying torches. The sea was too rough to leave by ship, and the smell of sulphur hung in the air, while the daylight did not return when morning should have come. Pliny's nephew, writing many years later, remembered that the darkness was worse than any ordinary night.

At Pompeii, light grey stones called pumice fell for many hours, and by the end they lay as deep as a tall man in some of the streets. The weight made roofs collapse, and many people ran from the town in panic, taking what they could carry, while others sheltered indoors and hoped that the storm would pass. About eighteen hours after the eruption began, the real killer came, and it was not the stones.

The next morning, a cloud of burning ash and gas rushed down the mountain at great speed and swept through the nearby towns. Anyone who had stayed in Pompeii or Herculaneum was killed, because no one could survive such heat, and the buildings and bodies were soon buried in thick layers of ash. Most of the people of Pompeii seem to have escaped in time, but archaeologists have still found the remains of more than a thousand victims there.

Pliny the Elder lay down on the beach at Stabiae to rest, and later he died, probably because he could not breathe the poisoned air, though no one is sure, since he was heavy and had weak lungs. His nephew wrote about the day in a letter to the historian Tacitus, and it is the only eyewitness account that we have, and it describes the cloud so well that experts still call such eruptions Plinian. It is a rare thing to be able to see an ancient disaster through the eyes of a witness.

The new emperor Titus sent officials to help the survivors, but the towns were never rebuilt, and over time people forgot exactly where they had been. In the eighteenth century workers began to dig them out, and later scholars poured plaster into the empty spaces left by the bodies, which gives us the shapes of the dead. Today Pompeii shows us daily life in a Roman town as no book can, while Rome itself, far away to the north, carried on as before.

A Roman citizen had three names, like Gaius Julius Caesar, which showed his personal name, his clan and his family branch, and these names were a badge of pride. For many people in the empire, being a citizen was a matter of great honour, and it was worth more than money or land. Having a place in the Roman world, with all the privileges that went with it, set a man apart from the common mass of subjects.

Citizens could vote in the assemblies, serve in the legions, make contracts under Roman law and appeal against unfair judgements to higher courts. They were also protected from some of the harshest punishments, which were used freely on slaves and foreigners, and a citizen accused of a serious crime could ask for a trial in Rome. These rights made the status valuable and gave it a legal meaning, quite apart from any honour.

Rome's allies in Italy had fought in its armies for centuries, but they were not citizens, and they had no voice in the decisions that sent them to war. In 91 BCE they rebelled in the conflict called the Social War, because they wanted the same rights and rewards as the Romans whom they had served so loyally. It was a bitter struggle, and for a while the survival of the republic seemed to be in doubt.

The Romans won the war, but they also realised that they could not simply defeat their neighbours for ever, so they gave way and offered citizenship to the Italian allies. Within a few years almost all free men in Italy were citizens, and the old distinction between Romans and Italians began to fade. It was a remarkable decision, because few conquering states in history have so willingly shared their power with those they defeated.

Rome also brought new people into the citizen body through the gift of freedom. A slave who was freed by a Roman citizen usually became a citizen himself, and his children would have full rights, which was unusual among ancient peoples and surprised many Greek visitors. Some of these freed people became rich businessmen, and their sons might even rise high in public life, although a few snobs looked down on them.

Roman soldiers from the provinces served in units called auxiliaries, and they were not citizens when they joined. After about twenty-five years of service they received a bronze certificate, which was a small, folded tablet that recorded their discharge, and it made them citizens, and for a time their children too. The certificate was precious, and many veterans took it home to their villages, where it served as proof of their new status for the rest of their lives.

The emperor Claudius was born in Gaul, at Lyon, and he argued that Rome had always grown stronger by welcoming outsiders, even those who had once been its enemies. In 48 CE he let rich Gauls enter the Senate, and part of his speech survives on a bronze tablet that was found in Lyon, so we can read much of what he said. Some senators were shocked, but the policy continued, and over time many provincials became senators and even emperors.

Under the emperor Trajan, the empire stretched from Britain in the north to the Persian Gulf in the east, and from the Danube to the deserts of Africa. In 117 CE it reached its greatest size, covering about two million square miles and holding perhaps sixty million people, though some of the new lands in the east were given up soon afterwards. It was a vast world that was held together by roads, laws, taxes and a shared language of government.

The next emperor, Hadrian, decided that Rome should protect its borders and not try to grow for ever, and he gave up some of Trajan's conquests. He travelled across the provinces for years, inspecting the frontier forts, and in 122 CE he began a long stone wall in northern Britain, parts of which can still be seen. Some Romans thought that this caution was weakness, but others believed that it was good sense.

Merchants, soldiers and farmers lived in towns from Syria to Spain, and they spoke Latin, Greek, Celtic and many other languages, worshipped hundreds of gods and kept their own local customs. Most of them were not citizens, so they had fewer rights than those who were, and this difference created a puzzle that the Romans had to solve sooner or later. How could one empire hold together if the people in it were not equal?

Septimius Severus, who came from North Africa, became emperor in 193 CE, and after his death in 211 CE his two sons were to rule together. The elder son, Caracalla, took his nickname from a long, hooded Gaulish cloak that he liked to wear, and he soon had his younger brother Geta murdered, so that he could rule alone. He was a harsh and suspicious man who relied on the army, and he spent much of his reign away from Rome.

In 212 CE Caracalla issued a decree that made almost all free people in the empire Roman citizens, from Britain to Egypt, and from Spain to Syria. It was one of the most important laws in Roman history, and it affected millions of people who suddenly became Romans overnight. The step is known as the Antonine Constitution, because Caracalla's official name was Antoninus, and it changed the meaning of the word Roman for ever.

Many people have asked why Caracalla did it, and the Roman historian Cassius Dio, who disliked the emperor, said that he wanted more money. Citizens had to pay certain taxes, including a tax on inheritance, and the number of tax payers would rise sharply, though other scholars point to a wish for unity. Nobody knows the exact reason, and Dio may well have exaggerated the emperor's selfish motives.

A part of the decree survives on a scrap of papyrus that was found in Egypt, and it is now kept in the German city of Giessen, where scholars still study it. Caracalla's full name was Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, and many of the new citizens took the name Aurelius in his honour, so that the name became extremely common across the empire. Historians can still trace thousands of men and women called Aurelius in the records of the following generations, which shows how widely the decree was felt.

The decree did not include slaves, who remained the property of their owners, and it also left out some peoples who had surrendered to Rome and had no status of their own. Nearly all free people in the empire now had the same legal standing, however, so the decree created a new kind of equality at the same moment as it left slavery untouched. The gap between those who were free and those who were not remained as wide as before.

Before the decree, being Roman had meant belonging to the city of Rome or, at least, to Italy, but now it meant having a legal status that could be held by anyone. A farmer in Egypt or a merchant in Britain could be just as Roman as a senator in the capital, and the law of Rome became the common law of a great part of the world. This idea, that law and not birth defines a person's rights, has influenced legal thinking ever since.

In practice the law still favoured the rich, whose punishments were lighter than those of the poor and who were more likely to win in court. So the decree gave people more rights on paper, but citizenship no longer felt as special as it once had, since a privilege that everyone shares is no longer a privilege. Some historians think that this loss of value was a hidden cost of the new policy.

In 235 CE the empire entered a dark period that historians call the third-century crisis. Armies fought each other, invaders crossed the frontiers, a deadly plague spread, and the emperors made their coins worse by mixing in cheap metal, so that prices rose and the old trade routes decayed. For the first time in centuries, the people of the empire had good reason to wonder whether Rome could survive.

In about fifty years more than twenty men were named emperor, and most of them were murdered or killed in battle, so that few reigned for more than a couple of years. Each new ruler had to buy the loyalty of his soldiers, and the soldiers could remove him whenever they chose, which made the system extremely unstable. The age of the long, secure reigns of Augustus and Hadrian had given way to an age of constant fear.

The Persians captured the emperor Valerian in 260 CE, and the empire split into three parts, with its own rulers in Gaul and in the East, and it seemed to be breaking up. The emperor Aurelian finally won the lost lands back in the 270s, and he also built a great wall around the city of Rome, which had not needed such protection for centuries. The empire had survived the storm, but it was no longer the same, and its next ruler would have to change it.

The empire had grown so large that no single emperor could rule it, and the generals who guarded the frontiers kept rebelling against him. In 284 Diocletian solved the problem by sharing power with three other rulers, each of whom controlled an army and a part of the empire, and he retired in 305 to a palace on the coast of the Adriatic. The arrangement worked for a time, but it also taught Romans to think of the empire as a set of separate parts.

Constantine, who became sole emperor in 324 after years of civil war, decided to build a new capital in the east, where the wealth and the danger both lay. He chose the old Greek city of Byzantium, on the Bosporus, where a strait links the Black Sea to the Mediterranean and where the site was easy to defend, and in 330 CE he renamed it Constantinople. The new city had walls, a great harbour, a hippodrome and a Senate of its own, and it soon rivalled the old capital in splendour.

When the emperor Theodosius died in 395, he left the empire to his two sons, one to rule in the east and one in the west, and it was never again united. The eastern half was richer, more crowded with cities and better protected by the water of the Bosporus, while the western half had fewer taxes, longer frontiers and more enemies. The two courts often quarrelled with each other, and each preferred to let the other bear the burden of a new invasion.

A people called the Huns rode out of the steppes of Asia and pushed many Germanic tribes in front of them, towards the Roman frontier, and the refugees were terrified. In 376 a large group of Goths asked permission to cross the Danube and settle in the empire, and the emperor, who needed soldiers and farmers, agreed to let them in. Roman officials, however, were corrupt and greedy, and the starving Goths were soon in a state of desperate anger.

The Goths were treated badly, and soon they rebelled and began to plunder the Balkans, defeating every army that came against them. At Adrianople in 378, they destroyed the Roman army and killed the emperor Valens, who was fighting in the front line, and about two-thirds of the soldiers died on the field. Rome had never suffered a disaster of this kind since Cannae, and this time there was no Scipio waiting to avenge it.

The Rhine was supposed to protect the western empire, but according to tradition, it froze on the last night of 406, and so the river became a road. Vandals, Alans and other tribes walked across the ice into Gaul, burning and plundering as they went, and the Romans, who had pulled troops out to fight elsewhere, could not stop them from going on into Spain. The great frontier that had stood for generations was gone almost overnight, and nothing could bring it back.

The Visigoths, under their king Alaric, marched into Italy, and in 410 CE they entered Rome through a gate that was opened at night, perhaps by traitors from inside. They plundered the city for three days, although they spared the major churches, and it was the first time in about eight hundred years that a foreign enemy had taken Rome, since the day that the Gauls had come. The emperor Honorius, safe in the marshes of Ravenna, was said to be more concerned about his pet hen, which was also called Roma.

The news of the sack spread all over the Roman world, and many people were deeply shocked, for they had believed that Rome would be safe for ever. Some blamed the new religion for angering the old gods, and a bishop in North Africa named Augustine wrote a long book called The City of God in reply, arguing that earthly cities are not permanent. His work shaped European thought for many centuries, and it began as a response to a disaster.

The empire was short of money and soldiers, so it pulled its troops out of the farthest provinces to defend the heart of Italy and Gaul. Traditionally about 410 CE, the legions left Britain, and the emperor told the British cities to look after themselves, a letter that historians still discuss with much heat. The island that Rome had held for more than three and a half centuries was left to its own devices, and soon new settlers began to arrive from across the North Sea.

In 451 Attila, the king of the Huns, invaded Gaul, and the next year he invaded Italy, but he turned back, and he died soon afterwards. In 455 the Vandals, who had taken Carthage some years before, sailed to Italy and plundered Rome for two weeks, carrying off treasure and many prisoners. By then the western emperors were often weak men chosen and removed by powerful generals, and the old authority of Rome was a mere shadow.

By 475 the real power in the west belonged to the generals, who were often of German origin and had risen through the army. One of them, Orestes, who had once served as a secretary to Attila, made his young son the emperor, and the boy was named Romulus, though people called him Augustulus, which means little Augustus. It was a strange irony that the last western emperor carried the name of the city's first king and of its first emperor.

Most of the army in Italy was made up of German soldiers, who were paid by Rome but wanted land to settle on and call their own. They asked for a third of the land of Italy, as other soldiers had received in earlier years, and Orestes refused, because he did not want to take so much from the Italian landowners. The soldiers, who felt cheated, began to look for another leader who would listen.

The soldiers rebelled, and they chose an officer named Odoacer, a capable officer, as their leader, and soon he had a great army behind him. He defeated Orestes in the summer of 476 and had him put to death, and the boy emperor, who was then probably about fifteen, was left without a protector. There was no one else in the west who had the strength or the will to fight for the throne.

Odoacer removed the young emperor from his throne in 476 CE, but he spared him, perhaps because the boy was so young and harmless, and he even gave him a pension. The boy was sent to live in a villa in southern Italy, and nobody knows for certain what happened to him afterwards, since he disappears from history. With his removal, the line of western emperors came to an end, and no one was appointed to take his place.

Odoacer sent the crown and purple robes of the western emperor to the eastern emperor Zeno in Constantinople, with the message that Italy no longer needed an emperor of its own. He went on to rule Italy as a king, and Zeno accepted this arrangement for the time being, since he had other problems and little ability to challenge it. In theory, there was only one Roman emperor, and he lived in the east.

Hardly anyone at the time believed that the Roman Empire had come to an end, since the Senate still met, the law courts still sat and farmers still took their goods to market. Italy was soon ruled by another king, Theodoric the Ostrogoth, who kept many Roman officials and respected Roman customs. Only later, looking back, did historians decide that the year 476 was a turning point.

The eastern half of the empire lasted for nearly a thousand years more, and its people always called themselves Romans, even though they spoke Greek. Today we call it the Byzantine Empire, and it recaptured parts of Italy under Justinian in the sixth century, but it fell only in 1453, when the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople. For its people, the fall of that city was the real end of Rome.

Historians still argue about why the western empire fell, and no single answer satisfies everyone. Some point to invasions and civil wars, others to weak money, plague and a government that had become too big to manage, while a few blame the loss of the old habits that had made the republic strong. The truth is probably a mixture of all these, and the question is still important because it asks how any great power can last.

Rome's gifts to the world were many, and Latin slowly turned into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, so that hundreds of millions of people speak its children today. Roman law, roads, aqueducts and concrete buildings, such as the great dome of the Pantheon, which is still the largest of its kind, are also a part of its legacy. Even our months of July and August are named after Julius Caesar and the emperor Augustus, whose stories we have followed in this book.

Today a visitor to Rome can walk past the ruins of the Forum, climb the Capitoline Hill where the geese once honked, and see the letters SPQR stamped on the manhole covers in the street. Caesar's name lives on in words such as Kaiser and tsar, and many modern legislatures still use the names of Roman institutions, such as Senate and Capitol. The story that began with a basket on a river never really ended, because we still live in the world that Rome helped to make.
